s01.slug: MONDAY · 6:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — THREE DAYS
body: The window over the landing between two and three is going from black to plum, and at the bottom edge, where the roof of the next building cuts it off, to a thin cold pink. Day twenty. Jack comes down the two flights from four with two Commons coffees in brown paper sleeves, one in each hand, and somewhere under the building a dryer that somebody started at midnight turns over, thumps, and settles back into its cycle.

She’s on her step in sweatpants and the Saints sweatshirt, knees up, a stack of index cards on them with a gumband round the middle. Hale’s three pages lie face down on the concrete beside her, the backward-leaning hand showing through the paper. Her hair is in a knot with a pencil through it. She has hardly slept since Saturday, and it shows under her eyes in two violet smudges, and the rest of her face hasn’t been told.

body.text: The top card says *2 MIN*. His note, her capitals, circled twice.
The top card says *DON’T BE CAST*, in her capitals.
The top card says *SAY IT TO HIS FACE*, in her capitals.
The top card says *owes* — and after it a long dash in pencil, the silence she means to leave.
The cards are face down under the gumband, and she has one thumb on them.

body: He holds a cup down to her. She takes it with her eyes still on the cards. “Thank you,” she tells them, and drinks, and makes the face Commons coffee has earned, and drinks again.
“You slept?”

“Some. I kept waking up and saying the first sentence to the ceiling. Laney threw a pillow at me at four and said if I said *owe* one more time she was going to owe me a black eye.” She drinks. She sounds happier about all of it than anybody who has slept four hours has a right to. “Three days.”
“Give me your watch.”

He unbuckles the Timex and hands it down. It goes on her wrist two holes too loose and slides to the knob of the bone, and she frowns at the face of it, and sets the cup on the step, and gets up and goes down to the landing to stand in front of the fire door to two. The wired glass is still dark enough to give her back to herself.
“Professor Hale is going to tell you that you owe each other everything,” she says. “He’ll be right. I want to ask him one question about the word.”

After that he stops hearing words and starts watching. He watches her right hand open on *debt* like she’s setting a dish on a table. He watches her chin come up toward the back row of a hall that isn’t here yet. He watches her not look at the cards on the step behind her even once, though she knows to the line what is on every one of them. He has heard her argue since August, on porches and in pews and down the length of an oak table, and this is something else: this is a woman who has stopped arguing and is telling you how it is.
“I only want to know who it’s owed to,” she says, and looks at the watch. “One fifty-two.”
“That’s under.”
“Again.”

She goes back to the top. This time, before the first word, she plants her feet a little apart on the concrete, the way a man plants them at a press on the line, and the first sentence goes out of her and into the door like a thing that has already happened.

“One forty-nine.” Over the landing the plum has gone out of the window and left the pink, and the pink is climbing. She looks at the watch on her wrist a second time, to make sure of it, and her whole face goes up at the corners and comes back down to business.
“You took three seconds off the debt,” he says.

“I took three seconds off *Hale*. The debt’s the same size it ever was.” She comes back up the half flight unbuckling his watch, scoops her coffee up off the step on the way, and stops a step below him with the watch held out on her other palm.
“Saturday. Where?”
“Mine.”
“You keep saying that like it’s a parish.”

choices.text: “It’s the closest thing I’ve got to one out here.”
response: She looks at him over the lid of her cup, longer than the line deserves. Then she comes up the one step between them, so close the two lids knock, and kisses him — quick, coffee and toothpaste — and goes back down to her own step and sits with the cards, as if she has put a period at the end of something.
He goes up the flight with his coffee in one hand and the watch, still warm, in the other, and at the top he couldn’t have told anybody how many stairs there were.

choices.text: “It has a softball team and a fish fry. You’ll see.”
response: “Fish fries are *Fridays*, Costigan. If there’s a fish fry on a Saturday in Lent, I am reporting it to somebody with a miter.”
She drops the Timex into his palm like a tip, and takes her cards back down to the fire door, and is already moving her lips at the wired glass, the first sentence, before he has the watch buckled.

choices.text: “You’ll laugh when you see it. I want you to.”
response: That lands somewhere he didn’t aim it. She doesn’t laugh now. She hooks a finger in the neck of his T-shirt and pulls him down the one step and kisses him, and lets go.
“Go away. I’m working, Youngstown.”
From the flight above he hears her start over from the top.

choices.text: *Don’t answer. Hand her the second coffee too.*
response: She takes it. Two coffees, one in each fist, and no hand left over for anything.
She kisses him anyway, quick, leaning out over both lids so as not to slop either one, and sits down on her step laughing at herself, looking up and down it for somewhere to put one of them.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE LAST MONDAY
body: The radiator under 302’s middle window is winning again, and the blinds are half down against a white sky that hasn’t decided about rain. Jack at the door end under the clock; Lena at the window end, a pencil going end over end in her fingers like a baton between movements. Caleb beside Jack in a clean shirt, knees already going. Yusuf beside Caleb. Evan Marsh in the doorway with the roster on its clipboard. At Hale’s elbow on the oak, a stack of new paperbacks with the price stickers still on, and on top of them *The Moviegoer*, closed, with about forty slips of paper sticking out of it.
Hale sits and looks round the table and lays down the law. “Anyone who says the word *Thursday* at this table will be made to read it aloud from the programme in a Welsh accent.”
Five minutes in, Caleb, making a point about Aunt Emily, says, “Which on *Thurs* —” and stops, and turns the color of a brake light.
“Does it count if I spell it?” Yusuf says.

“It counts double. Spelling is how the Welsh got into this.” Hale opens *The Moviegoer* at the last of the slips. “So. A farewell to Binx Bolling. Ash Wednesday. He sits in his car outside the church on Elysian Fields with Kate beside him and watches a man come down the steps with the ashes on his forehead, and he cannot say — Percy will not let him say — whether the man has come for God, or because it’s good for business to be seen there, or both at once, by some trick of grace. Percy, being a Catholic, refuses to tell us. Percy, being a novelist, is right not to. Discuss.”

They discuss. A sophomore with a nose ring says Binx is a tourist in his own life; another says he’s depressed and the book thinks that’s deep. “Everyone in New Orleans is depressed in August,” Hale says. “Percy merely wrote it down.” From the window end, without lifting her pencil: “We’re not depressed, Professor. We’re humid.” The sophomores laugh, and Hale inclines his head toward the window. It is as much ground as he gives anybody before a fight. Caleb, recovered, says with all his Central Valley chest that the search is the point — that Binx says somewhere that not to be onto something is to be in despair, and the man on the steps is onto something whether Binx can see it or not — and Hale lets him have three sentences, two more than usual. Lena, later, says one thing about the man on the steps: that Binx is the only person in that scene who thinks it matters why the man came, and that wondering about it might be the nearest Binx has got to a prayer. Then she goes back to her pencil.

Across the oak her eyes keep starting for the clock. It is over his head, and every time her eyes come up the table they have to come past him to get to it, and they don’t get to it; they stop on him and go back down to the pencil. She’s writing in the margin of her Percy in very small capitals. From the door end he can’t read a word of it, and he would bet the tip jar that none of it is about Binx.
Hale doesn’t look at her for long. He doesn’t look at the door end for long either. He looks, mostly, at the book.

“Thirty years,” he says, “Binx doesn’t turn up to his own life. He goes to the pictures. He sells mutual funds. Percy keeps him on the page regardless.” He turns a slip over with one finger. “A man may miss a Thursday and still be in the story.”
The sophomores take it as Percy. At the window end Lena’s pencil stops for the length of the sentence and then goes on. Jack, under the clock, doesn’t take it as Percy at all.

Hale lays a hand on the stack of paperbacks. “After the event this table does not name: Waugh. *Brideshead*. Catholic, English and drunk. Two out of three, and I leave you to guess which.” The table laughs. He waits it out. “Mr. Costigan. You’ve been quiet. Is Binx saved, or merely self-aware?”

choices.text: “The man on the steps went up for ashes, and nobody can say why. Probably not him either. That’s most of us, sir.”
response: Hale considers him over his glasses. “Most of *you*, Mr. Costigan.”
At the window end Lena writes something down, and underlines it.

choices.text: “He’s saved. He just hasn’t been told yet. It’s a very Catholic position.”
response: The table laughs. “The Church’s most comfortable doctrine,” Hale says. “Salvation by post.”
Caleb writes *salvation by post* on the back of his hand.

choices.text: “Self-aware. Percy wants you to think it’s the same thing. It isn’t.”
response: “Good,” Hale says — just the word — and moves on to the nose ring, and it is the most he has given Jack across that table since February.
Over Jack’s head the clock lurches to 2:14.

body: The chairs go back. The sophomores get into their coats, and somebody knocks the stack of *Brideshead*s over and stands it up again, and Hale, writing in the margin of *The Moviegoer* with his fountain pen, says, “Mr. Costigan. A word.”

Lena, at the door with her bag on her shoulder, looks back at Jack. In a moment she’s down the hall toward the stairs, and Caleb is gone after her with his question about Aunt Emily, and the room is two men, a radiator, and a lot of oak.
Jack stays standing. Hale doesn’t ask him to sit.
Hale finishes his sentence in the margin first. Whatever it is takes him four lines in the tall backward hand, and he reads it over, and doesn’t seem to think much of it.
“Will you be at Sandoval on Thursday?”
He says the word himself, at his own table, and there is no fine.
“Yes, sir.”
“Sit where she can see you.” The pen goes on moving. Up at the tops, Hale’s ears have gone faintly red. “Not where I can.”
Jack doesn’t say anything to that. There isn’t anything a man could say to it that Hale would forgive him for.

“The Dean,” he says, briskly, still writing, “has asked me to wear a microphone on the night. A little clip on the lapel, with a cord down one’s back like a tail. I have told her I have never in my career needed help to be heard, and that if the back row can’t hear me they may come down to the front like everyone else.” He turns the page. “Miss Broussard will not need one either. I have been on the receiving end of that voice since September.”

Jack stands there with his bag on his shoulder. Out the middle window the quad is going white under the sky that hasn’t made up its mind, and a kid in a wetsuit pulled down to the waist is crossing it barefoot with a board, as if Hollis were the beach.

“You made a very passable me last Monday,” Hale says. “Don’t do it again this week. She has had quite enough of me. And read the Waugh. Everyone in it is Catholic and miserable, which I’m told is accurate.”
“She came to my office on Friday to tell me which two of my three pages were wrong. She was right about one of them.” He says it to the margin, and it costs him a tooth.

That’s all. Hale turns a page. Jack waits long enough to be sure, and then gets his bag up onto his shoulder and goes to the door, past the radiator ticking under the middle window and the *Brideshead*s with their price stickers, and has his hand on the cold brass of the knob when Hale, capping the pen, says without looking up:
“Thursday last. I’m told you were in Ohio.”

choices.text: “I was in a parked car, owing somebody an explanation. I paid it.”
choices.key: When Hale asked about the Thursday you missed, you told him you’d been in a parked car paying a debt.
response: Hale looks up at that, and this time he looks at Jack and not at the margin.
“And was it accepted?”
“Not yet.”

“Then you’ve learned what a debt is.” He sets the pen down. “Miss Broussard has been trying to teach it to me for a week. She is a better teacher than I was at her age, and much less pleasant to argue with. Go away, Mr. Costigan.”

choices.text: “Someone needed the truth, slowly. It took the afternoon.”
choices.key: When Hale asked about the Thursday you missed, you told him someone had needed the truth, slowly.
response: Hale is quiet. He sets the capped pen down across *The Moviegoer*, and looks at the stack of Waugh instead of at Jack, and the radiator is the only thing talking in the room.
“There are worse reasons to miss a seminar,” he says. “I’ve used most of them. None of them took the afternoon.”
Jack lets himself out.

choices.text: “Ohio, sir. The entire state.”
choices.key: When Hale asked about the Thursday you missed, you told him you’d been in Ohio — the entire state.
response: “That was my line,” Hale says. “Miss Broussard delivered it better, and with less sweat.”
Jack is on the stairs grinning before he’s out of the room, and halfway down he isn’t, because a man who remembers his own line from a week ago remembers what face it got.

choices.text: “It won’t happen again.”
choices.key: When Hale asked about the Thursday you missed, you told him it wouldn’t happen again.
response: Hale finally looks up. He looks at Jack in the doorway with his bag on his shoulder, the way he looks at a premise somebody has offered him with a straight face.
“It will,” Hale says. “See that it’s worth it.”

s03.slug: MONDAY · 3:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY — UNDER B
body: The afternoon has come round to the front of Delgado and lies across the lobby floor in long tilted panes, and the mailboxes’ little brass doors throw it up onto the ceiling in coins. On the bulletin board, between the dryer flyer and a sign-up for intramural inner-tube water polo, somebody from the Forum committee has pinned a flyer with HALE in one column and BROUSSARD in the other, and somebody else has drawn a very small halo over her name in blue ballpoint and, over his, a very small pair of horns. The Yellow Pages is back on its shelf under the board, where it was a week ago. Jack takes it down and stands with it open on his forearm and finds what he’s looking for under B, and runs his thumb down the column, and stops.
The lobby phone is a beige box on the wall by the mailboxes with a cord that has been stretched by every homesick freshman since the building went up. It’s free, and his minutes aren’t. He dials.

It rings five times. A man picks up with a television going behind him — a ball game, a crowd, somebody selling trucks — and says the name of the place like he has said it ten thousand times and would like to say it ten thousand more.

Jack tells him what he wants. Saturday night. Two people. After six, if they can. He says it better than he said *a table for two* last week; he’s had practice now, and this time the place isn’t going to want a jacket.
“Sixteen,” the old man says. “By the wall. Nobody wants it, the return sticks. Saturday after six it’s yours.”
“Sixteen’s good.” Then, because he’s got the man on the line: “Does your grill do shrimp?”

The man laughs, a big laugh with a cough at the bottom of it. “Ask Connie,” he says, and hangs up, and the ball game goes with him. Jack hangs the receiver back on its hook and stands there with the Yellow Pages open on his arm, smiling at the bulletin board like a fool, at the halo and the horns.

The sophomore at the desk is doing calculus. She has a column of derivatives going down the back of a Res Life flyer and her lips are moving, and when Jack borrows a Bic off her counter and writes *16* on the back of his hand she says “mm” and keeps going.

There’s been rain since before light, and more coming. Morro 1100’s long windows are beaded from the sills halfway up, and what comes through them is a wet green-white, the light of a room at the bottom of a pool. Jack climbs the tiers at five to eleven shaking the drizzle off the Carhartt and finds Skye already there, back row under the exit sign, her bag on the floor on her own side.
“Hi,” she says, before he has sat down.

Jeans, the navy sweater, her hair back in a tortoiseshell clip with the ends coming out of it, no makeup he can find. She smells of the rain and of the grapefruit stuff she uses in her hair, and he knows that, and would rather he didn’t know it quite so well.
Down at the board Dr. Fenner has drawn the sun, the earth and the moon in a straight line, three circles on a string.
“Spring tide,” he says, and taps the string. “Who can tell me why it’s called spring?”
A girl in the second row says because it happens in the spring.

“It does not. It happens twice a month, every month, in January, in a blizzard.” He beams. “Spring has nothing to do with the season. It’s the water *springing* up. Sun and moon pulling the same way — new moon, full moon — highest highs, lowest lows. New moon’s next week. Go look at the harbor pilings.” He taps the quarter moons. “Neap. That’s when they’re pulling against each other and nobody gets what they want.” The joke dies at the board, and he is happy anyway.

When Fenner calls the conferences, the desks bang down all along the tiers, and she already has the project out: a sheet of graph paper with the Point traced off the chart, the depth lines curving round under the headland in pencil, and over them, in four colors of felt-tip, the wave rays coming in straight from the open sea — blue, green, orange, red — and bending as the bottom comes up under them, crowding onto the reef off the Point like people at a door and thinning out across the cove beyond.

“The bottom slows them,” she says, and runs the cap of her pen along a blue line. The cap is chewed flat. “Whatever part of the wave feels the shallow water first slows down first, and the rest of it swings round to catch up. So they wrap. Everything piles onto the Point. That’s why it breaks there and nowhere else in the bay.” She turns the sheet to face him. “I did the swell angles. You do the math. You’re the one who likes math.”

He does the math. A wave in shallow water goes at the square root of gravity times the depth, which means the part of a swell crossing ten feet of reef is doing half the speed of the same swell over forty, and the slow end drags and the fast end swings round on it like a gate on a post. He writes it out under her colors in pencil. She checks it upside down, faster than he did it, and finds one thing, and is right.
Fenner comes up the side stairs with his clipboard, ticking pairs, and stops at the top and bends over the graph paper and its four colors with his reading glasses pushed up on his forehead.
“Both halves,” he says. “Good.” And goes back down, pleased with the world.

“That’s going on my headstone,” Skye says, watching him go. “*Both halves. Good.* Under the dates. People will come from miles.” It gets a laugh out of him. She caps the felt-tip. “You laughed. That’s one.”
At a quarter past twelve the room empties down the tiers around them, umbrellas and zippers and somebody arguing about a lab, and she reaches into her bag and sets a book square on his open notebook.

It’s the paperback from her dash: *Catechism of the Catholic Church*, thick as a phone book for a small town, a Borders sale sticker on the cover with the price struck through, and the receipt that was sticking out of it on Thursday moved up to page one.

The only catechism Jack owns is the Baltimore, No. 2, in his desk drawer under the tip envelope: *Who made us? God made us*, fits in a shirt pocket, his own name in the front in a second-grader’s capitals. This one would hold a door open in a high wind.
“It was on sale,” she says. “It’s the only reason I could afford the highlighters.”
He looks at it, and at her.
“You said what you’re for,” Skye says. “I want to read the manual.”
“Don’t do the face.”
“What face?”
“The one where you’re about to be fair to me. Not yet.” She taps the cover with one finger.
“From the beginning. In order. One section at a time.”
“Skye —”

“I read the overture already. The prologue. On Sol’s porch, Sunday, with a blanket. It’s mostly about why the book exists, which every book should have to explain.” She ticks something off on her fingers. “I’m doing it because you said a thing to me I didn’t understand, and I don’t like that, and there’s a book. Either you talk me into it or I talk you out of it. I’m not picky which.”
“A priest would —”
“— be better at this. Better at the answers, sure. I don’t want the answers from somebody who’s never had to lose anything over them.” She doesn’t wait to see if that lands.
“Wednesdays. Four. Low Tide — the surf shop with the menu on a board. We were always going to study for this anyway.” She taps the graph paper. “Daylight. In public.”

body.text: She points her pen at him. “The daylight column. Your priest’s.”
body.else: She spreads her hands. “Nobody can say a word about four in the afternoon.”

body: And, in a late-night voice off a channel in the high numbers, a man in a headset selling knives at two in the morning: “But wait. There’s more.” She lays her palm on the cover. “It’s two thousand eight hundred and sixty-five paragraphs. I counted the last one. I did the math. It’s years.”
“And?”
She takes her hand off the book and puts the cap back on her pen.
“I’ve got till May in this class,” she says, “and the rest of my life after that.”

The room has emptied out under them while she talked. Down at the bottom of the tiers Fenner is fitting his overheads back into their box one at a time, humming, and the long windows have started to run, and the book sits on Jack’s notebook between his two hands with the receipt sticking out of page one like a tongue.

choices.text: “Okay. From the beginning.”
choices.key: When Skye asked to argue the whole Catechism with you, one section at a time, you said yes — from the beginning.
response: “That’s two things you’ve said I didn’t have to pull out of you.”
She puts the book away in her bag, spine down, the receipt still sticking out of page one, and gets the bag up onto her shoulder.

choices.text: “I’ll be telling Lena.”
choices.key: When Skye asked to argue the whole Catechism with you, you said yes, and told her you’d be telling Lena.
response: She doesn’t blink.
“You tell people things,” she says. “It’s your worst quality.”

She picks up the book and goes, down the side stairs with it under her arm. Jack sits on in the back row under the exit sign with his notebook, which is only a notebook again, and the warm place on it where the book was.

choices.text: “You’ll quit at the Trinity.”
choices.key: When Skye asked to argue the whole Catechism with you, you bet her she’d quit at the Trinity.
response: “I’ll *thrive* at the Trinity.” She takes the book back and stands. “The Father, the Son and a bird. I’ve worked with worse ensembles.”

choices.text: “Wednesday.”
choices.key: When Skye asked to argue the whole Catechism with you, you said yes, and named the day — Wednesday.
response: “Wednesday,” she says.

She takes the book and goes, down the side stairs. Her seat folds itself up behind her with a clack, and Jack caps his pen and puts it away in the spine of his notebook with a good deal more care than a Bic has ever needed.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 4:30 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — THE EMPTY STAGE

body.text: Sandoval 1, 4:30. Come see where I’ll be standing. —L.
ill be there. i have to tell you something first

body: Sandoval Hall 1 with nobody in it is four hundred orange flip-down seats going up into the dark, the house lights at half, and one worklight on a stand at the side of the stage that makes everything on the boards hard and white and everything off them brown. Up in the ceiling the air handler runs on, steady, the only sound in the building. It’s the room where Hale taught PHIL 1 to both of them in the fall. On the stage, two lecterns with a bare table between them; Thursday’s pitcher isn’t out yet.

Lena is on the stage in her socks. Her flats are side by side on the lip of it, toes out, and she is walking the boards slowly, heel to toe, with her chin tilted, listening. Her cards and Hale’s three pages are on her lectern. Coiled on Hale’s, stage right, is the little clip-on microphone Hale won’t wear, its black cord wound in a neat figure eight. She reaches the front of his lectern and a board answers her, and she stops on it and rocks, and it says it again.

He stands at the top of the aisle with the door easing shut behind him and lets her find the next one. She hasn’t seen him yet. She is mouthing something as she walks, her lips going, one hand making a small shape in the air at her side and putting it away again, and the worklight throws her shadow off the back of the stage and up the wall behind her twice her size.
She looks up and finds him in the aisle. “You came.”
“I have to tell you something first.”

It’s a long aisle. He has had since a quarter past twelve with it — through a Commons tray he pushed around and didn’t eat, and twenty minutes on the bench outside Sandoval with his hands between his knees and the bells in Ferrer doing the half hour — and all the way down the steps he can feel her up there on the boards, watching him come and not asking.
He takes the front row, dead center, and the seat lets him know about it. She stays where she is, on Hale’s board. Whatever she had ready to say about Thursday she puts away.

“Skye bought a Catechism,” he says. “The big one, the paperback. She wants to read it from page one and argue it with me as she goes. A section at a time. In public. For as long as it takes.” After all that he still hasn’t worked out how to say it, and says it anyway, in the order it happened. “She asked me at noon, after Oceanography. I said yes.” He makes himself put in the rest of it, the part that’s true and doesn’t help. “We’re partners in Fenner’s class till May. We were going to be studying together anyway, coffee after class. This is on top of that. I didn’t want you to get it from anybody else, or from a week from now.”

Lena doesn’t move. She stands under the worklight in her socks with her weight on the creaking board and doesn’t let it creak. While he talks her right hand has found the microphone on Hale’s lectern, and the cord, and has wound the cord once round two fingers.
“When?”
“Tomorrow. Every Wednesday. Four o’clock.”
“Where?”
“Low Tide.” The cord goes round her fingers a second time.
“The surf shop with the menu on a board.” She has it placed; he watches her put it on the map, the bike path, the window, the boards up the walls. “What does she want?”
“To understand it. Or to talk me out of it.”
“She can’t.”
“No.”

She doesn’t say anything for a while after that. She looks out past him at the empty house, at the seats going up into the dark where the worklight doesn’t reach, and in all that quiet he can hear her breath, slow and even, going in and coming out. Inside the cord the tips of those fingers have gone white. On her lectern her cards sit in their gumband under the worklight, where she left them. He sits in the front row and waits for whatever she’s going to ask. He knows already what he’ll say to it, and that he can’t say it until she has.

body.text: “You told me Thursday she said it isn’t done,” she says. “I heard you.”
“You told me Thursday some of it was hers,” she says. “I let you keep it. I’m still letting you.”
“You told me Thursday you told her the truth,” she says. “I believed you. I still do.”
“She was always going to want more than a car,” she says.

body: She unwinds the cord from her fingers a turn at a time, and lays it back on Hale’s lectern in its figure eight, exactly as it was, and takes her hand away. She looks down at him in the front row.
“Then here’s mine.”
Her voice is as level as the stage.
“If she ever makes a move, it stops. The coffees, the book, all of it. Promise me.”
“I promise.”

He says it straight back up to her, with nothing on either side of it. Up in the ceiling the air handler cycles off, and the quiet it leaves is bigger than the hall. She stays where she is, on the creak, and hears it.

choices.text: “You’d have heard about the book before anybody. You did.”
choices.key: On the empty stage, you told Lena about Skye’s Catechism before anyone else could, and made her the promise she asked for.
response: “I know,” Lena says. “That’s why I can stand up here.”

She says it to him alone. Then she lifts her chin, there in her socks on Hale’s board, with the empty house in front of her and him in the first row of it, the medal catching the worklight at her collarbone, and he looks.

choices.text: “She’s going to try to argue me out of it. Not — that. The faith.”
choices.key: On the empty stage, you made Lena the promise she asked for, and told her plainly that Skye meant to argue you out of your faith.
response: “Let her try,” Lena says.

There’s no heat in it, and no boast. She says it about God the way she’d tell you the river comes up in April — not a hope, not a dare, a thing she has watched happen all her life from the top of a levee. She stands on the creaking board and looks down at him, her empty hands at her sides.

choices.text: *Say nothing more. Let the promise stand by itself.*
choices.key: On the empty stage, you made Lena the promise she asked for, and let it stand without another word.
response: He leaves it where it is, in the big room.
She looks at him from the stage a good while, under the worklight, with her hands at her sides and her weight on the board that creaks, and it doesn’t. Then she nods, once.

choices.text: “Do your first two minutes for me. I’ll be the room.”
choices.key: On the empty stage, you made Lena the promise she asked for, and then asked her to give you her first two minutes — and she did.
response: She looks at him, and at the empty house behind him, and crosses to her own lectern in her socks, and doesn’t touch the cards.

She starts with the sentence he heard at the fire door at dawn, and it isn’t the same sentence anymore. After that he doesn’t hear it as words. He hears the room she’s talking to — the one that isn’t there yet, all of Thursday — going quiet for her a row at a time, and he is the house, every seat of it, in one.
When she finishes she stands with one hand on the lectern and looks down at him over it, waiting to hear what the room thought.

s05a.slug: TUESDAY · 4:55 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — FRONT ROW, CENTER
body: She comes down the stage steps at the side in her socks, one hand on the rail, and sits in the seat next to his. The seat says the same thing his did. For a little they sit there an armrest apart, the worklight up on the stage throwing their two shadows out long across the carpet in front of them, and then she leans, and her shoulder settles against his.

body.text: “Better?” she says.
“Better.”
She doesn’t run it again. She sits with her shoulder against his and looks at the stage the way she’d look at a kitchen she means to cook Christmas in.

She doesn’t stand up for it. She says the first sentence from where she is, sitting down, without the cards, low, to the dark at the top of the house — and it’s better than at the fire door this morning: slower, with the weight on *one question*, as if there might really be only the one and she’s sorry for him about it.

body: “Hale walks,” she says. “He puts his hands behind his back and goes up and down like he’s reviewing troops. I’m not going to walk. I’m going to stand on his board and let it creak every time I lean on him.” She looks at the boards. “I’ll have to lean on him a fair amount.”
“You will.”

“Mama made me learn every stage in my socks. The parish hall at Christmas, the gym for the spelling bee. She says you have to know where the floor is going to talk back before you let anybody watch you stand on it.” She wiggles her toes in the socks. They are navy, with a hole coming at one heel. “The building manager gave me an hour and a long talk about not touching the worklight.”
“Did you touch the worklight?”
“I moved it four feet. It was lighting the wrong lectern.”
“And don’t clap when he’s funny,” she says. “He’s going to be very funny. He’s going to be funny from his first sentence to his last, and the house is going to love him for it.”
“I’ll clap when you’re funny.”
“You’ll be sitting on your hands, then. I don’t plan on being funny.” She tips her head back against the seat and looks up at the dark where the ceiling must be.
“Thursday. Third row. Aisle.”
“Why the third row?”
“So I can find you without looking for you.”

She leans forward out of the seat and gets her flats off the lip of the stage and stands, and he gets his knees out of her way. She has the rest of an hour to give back to the building manager. She goes up the aisle in her socks between the orange seats with her shoes in one hand, not hurrying, past the third row, past all of them, toward the doors at the top, where the light from the lobby is.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 11:40 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE DISH RACK
body: Twenty to midnight on a Tuesday, and the Anchor is down to the light over the pie case and the coffee on its burner. Two fishermen are in early for the boats, at the far end of the counter in their white rubber boots, eating eggs with their caps on and not talking. Rudy’s radio is going on its shelf over the grill, low, three men singing close together over a guitar, and Rudy scrapes down the flattop in long strokes that keep time with it.

Jack has been in the back since seven with the Hobart. His forearms are pink to the elbow and the tips of his fingers have gone soft and white and ridged. He shoulders through the kitchen door with a rack of clean cups, and Kevin Tran is sitting at the counter.

Kevin doesn’t come to the Anchor alone. He comes with the group, in the van, and orders toast, and holds the keys, and gets everybody home; he made himself the fourth floor’s designated adult the first week of September and hasn’t been off duty since. He’s in his good quarter-zip, the navy one with the little Marisol crest, zipped to the collarbone, and he is alone, sitting very straight on the stool with his hands folded on the Formica in front of him. His BlackBerry is face down by the napkins. Out the window his mother’s Odyssey is parked under the lot light across two spaces. It is the first thing Jack has ever seen Kevin do crooked.

Gloria sees him from the pass. She looks at him once over the order wheel and puts down the ticket in her hand, and pours a coffee, and cuts a slice of the coconut cream, and sets both of them in front of him before anybody has said a word.
“On the house,” she says. “Don’t argue with me, I’m older than your mother.”
“I wasn’t going to argue.”
“You were thinking about it.” She goes back to her tickets.

Kevin watches her go. “I drove out to the lighthouse first,” he says to Jack. “And back. Twice.” He lines the fork up beside the saucer. “I didn’t want to go back to the floor yet.” He looks down at the plate. “I’ve never had the coconut cream. I always get the toast.” He turns the saucer a little toward the light. “Clinically, it presents well.”

Jack sets the rack down on the counter by the coffee station, forty cups upside down in their grid, still giving off a little steam. Kevin looks at Jack’s hands on the rack. “Those are macerated,” he says. “That’s a medical term. It means pruney. You should be wearing gloves.” He looks back at the rack.

“Clare ended it,” he says. “Tonight. In the Newman kitchen, by the dish rack.” He nods at the one in front of him. “Smaller than that. Same idea.” He picks up the coffee and puts it down again without drinking any. “She made me tea first. She had the kettle on before I got my coat off. I should have known right there. Clare doesn’t believe in tea.”
Jack wipes his hands on the towel at his hip. He thinks of Sunday, two pews up: Clare reaching up with both hands to fix Kevin’s collar where it had gone under on one side.
Behind the pass Rudy has stopped scraping. He doesn’t turn around. He stands at the flattop with the scraper in his hand, listening to the radio, or to the counter.

“She was very kind about it,” Kevin says. “She’d thought about what she was going to say. She had it in order, like she marks up the music for Sunday.” He picks up the fork. “She said I’m a very good man who’s never in the room.”
He cuts the slice into eight even pieces with the side of the fork before he eats any of it. He eats the first one, and chews it for exactly as long as it needs.
“Respectfully — she’s right.”
He smiles at Jack, the smile he does for photographs, and eats the second piece.

Out in the lot somebody’s truck turns over twice and catches. The fishermen put their money down under their plates and go out into the noise of it, and the bell over the door rings behind them, and the room is the three of them and Rudy and the radio.

Kevin eats the third piece. “My mom was going to have her for Easter,” he says. “She bought a ham already. It’s in the garage freezer in Fremont with Clare’s name on a Post-it.” He thinks about it. “Her brothers are going to be so relieved. They’re very large.”
He eats the fourth piece. “Don’t tell Laney,” he says. “She’ll organize something.”

Jack can see it from here: a sign-up sheet on 217’s door by breakfast, a casserole rota, a card going round with everybody’s name on it in different pens. Kevin puts the fifth piece in his mouth and looks past him at the pie case, where the lemon meringue is sweating under the light.

choices.text: “I’m sorry, Kev.”
choices.key: When Kevin came to the Anchor after Clare ended it, you told him you were sorry.
response: “I’m sorry, Kev.”
Kevin nods at the pie, slowly, before he answers. “Me too,” he says. “For her.”
Gloria reaches over from the pass with the pot and fills his cup to the brim without asking him, and goes back to her tickets.

choices.text: “You drove to the lighthouse twice instead of going home. That’s not nothing, Kev.”
choices.key: When Kevin came to the Anchor after Clare ended it, you told him the two drives to the lighthouse weren’t nothing.
response: “You drove to the lighthouse twice instead of going home,” Jack says. “That’s not nothing, Kev.”
Kevin looks up from the pie and straight at him. “It’s a symptom,” he says. “Of a breakup. They’re very well documented.”
He holds his cup out anyway, and Gloria fills it from the pass, and Kevin sits with both hands around it and his thumbs on the rim, holding on to the one hot thing in reach.

choices.text: “Gloria, he’s going to need the second slice.”
choices.key: When Kevin came to the Anchor after Clare ended it, you got Gloria to cut him a second slice.
response: “Gloria,” Jack says, “he’s going to need the second slice.”
Gloria is already cutting it. She slides it down the counter on its saucer, and it stops against the first one with a little clink.
Kevin laughs. It comes out of him loud and short and surprised, and he gets a hand up over his mouth too late, and sits there at the counter of the Anchor at midnight with his fork up in the air.

choices.text: *Stack the cups. Let him eat.*
choices.key: When Kevin came to the Anchor after Clare ended it, you let him eat in peace.
response: Jack stacks the cups on the shelf over the coffee station, four rows of ten, handles all one way. Kevin eats the rest of the pie, in order, and drinks the coffee, and says nothing else, and Jack doesn’t make him.
At 12:20 he gets up and leaves a ten under the saucer for a slice that was free, folded small, the way you’d leave an apology, and Jack lets him.
He zips the quarter-zip the last inch at the door. The bell goes. “Night, hon,” Gloria says from the pass, with her eyes on a ticket.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:55 PM · LOW TIDE, LAS OLAS — THE GOWN
body: At noon it’s raining on the window of Driftwood Books on Mission, a fine rain that beads and doesn’t run, and Boethius is asleep on the register on top of the receipt pad. In Religion, under a shelf of Merton, there’s a *Catechism of the Catholic Church*, the fat paperback, with *$4* penciled inside the cover and somebody else’s pencil all through it: a neat line under the first sentence of paragraph twenty-seven, and a page on, in the margin by thirty, in a small slanting hand, *yes*. Jack pays at the register, around the cat.

The rain has quit by four, and Las Olas is steaming a little in a thin sun. Low Tide is a block in from Seacliff Road where the bike path comes out of the Grove, in what used to be a surf shop and hasn’t entirely given it up. The board racks are still up the walls with three or four old longboards left in them, yellowed, dinged at the rails. The menu is painted on another one, hung sideways behind a counter of varnished plywood. The espresso machine has a Post-it on its chrome that says DOLORES. At eight in the morning, Jack has heard, the place is wall-to-wall wetsuits. At four on a Wednesday it’s the barista, a girl with a nose ring and an iPod plugged into the stereo; two surfers in hoodies arguing about a swell at the table under the racks; a song with a warped, swaying organ in it; and, at the back table by the window onto the bike path, Skye.
She picked it. It isn’t anybody’s place: daylight, a long window, people going by on bicycles, the smell of espresso and surf wax and wet concrete.

She’s in a gown. Black silk, cut in one long column for a premiere and held up by two straps no wider than a bootlace; when she turns her head toward the door it turns out there’s nothing to the back of it, not down to the waist — only her back, the long groove of her spine and the light off the wet window lying along it. On the side toward him the slit runs to the hip. Her hair is up, pinned high, done by somebody who does hair for a living. At her ears there are two diamonds the size of chickpeas. Under the table, on the concrete, a pair of gold heels lies on its side where she stepped out of them.
It’s four o’clock on a Wednesday, at a plywood table, in a surf shop.

The barista misses the cup. The steamed milk goes over the side and across the counter, and she doesn’t notice until it’s dripping off the edge. A kid with a skateboard under his arm gets as far as the doorway behind Jack, stops, looks, and backs out onto the sidewalk the way he came. Under the racks one of the surfers says, “— it’s not gonna be overhead, dude, it’s gonna be —” and doesn’t finish, and his friend doesn’t need him to.
It’s obvious, and it’s very funny.
She gets there first.
“Yes. It’s a strategy. It isn’t a subtle strategy. I’m committed to it.”
“Sit down.”
There’s a coffee already on his side of the table, black, in a thick white mug with a chip out of the handle. He sits down in front of it.

He looks. He’s made of the usual parts, and they answer all of it at once without consulting him — the bare back, the silk, the long line of the slit — and he gets his eyes up to her face, and her face is laughing at him.
“*Sweetwater*,” she says, when his eyes get to her ears. “The wedding episode. Wardrobe never asked for them back.”

And then for ten minutes she doesn’t mention any of it. She has Fenner’s worksheet out — SPRING AND NEAP TIDES, PAIR 41 — and her half of the refraction project, the Point drawn in four colors of ink with the wave rays bending around it like combed hair, and she wants his half of the math, and she wants it right. He hands it over. She reads it with her chin on her fist.

“Five point eight minus negative nine-tenths,” she says, “is not four point nine. It’s six point seven. You subtracted the minus. And number three’s backwards. Spring is new and full. Neap is the quarters.” When he still looks doubtful she builds it for him on the plywood: a sugar packet for the sun, a creamer for the earth, a pink packet for the moon. “Lined up, they pull together. Big tides. Spring.” She slides the pink packet a quarter of the way round. “Right angles, they cancel. Neap. Fenner’s going to ask.” She writes it in for him in a small fast hand, and one strap slides off her shoulder, and she hitches it back up with one finger and goes on to number four.

When the worksheet is done it goes in its folder and the folder goes in her bag, and out of the bag comes a binder two inches thick with tabs down the side in her capitals — DESIRE · KNOWING · SPEAKING · REVELATION, and on down past where he can read — and three highlighters, capped, laid in a row along the top of it.
“Yellow, I agree,” she says, touching each one. “Pink, I don’t. Green —” she taps it — “this is a good line, which isn’t the same thing.”

Her own copy is new, the spine barely cracked, the Borders sale sticker on the cover and a receipt in it for a bookmark. “Highlighters,” she says, when she sees him look at the sticker, as if that settles something. Beside the sticker, in a little roundel, a shepherd sits under a tree with a sheep at his feet, playing a set of pipes. She turns it so he can see. “Your mascot plays the flute.”
She opens it where the receipt is, lays the receipt in the gutter with one finger, and looks up at him, all business.
“Page one.”

choices.text: “You’re overdressed for the desire for God.”
response: “You’re overdressed for the desire for God.”
“I’m dressed *exactly* right for the desire for God.” She looks him over once — the Carhartt, the T-shirt under it, the hair the wind got to on the walk from the bus. “You’re underdressed.”
He looks down at the Carhartt and has nothing to say for himself.

choices.text: “You know I’m going to look.”
response: “You know I’m going to look.”
“You can look.” She doesn’t reach for a strap or a napkin or anything else. “Looking’s in the strategy. Page one.”
He looks down at the open book, at paragraph twenty-seven, and eventually, a sentence or two in, he is actually reading it.

choices.text: *Open to ¶27. Read the first line out loud.*
response: He opens his own copy, the four-dollar one, to the stranger’s pencil line, and reads the first sentence aloud, to the print.
She lets him get to the end of it.
“You read like a man in a hostage video,” she says. “Again. With feeling.”
He reads it again, with feeling, badly, with his eyes on the pencil line from the first word to the last.

body: “Rules,” she says. “One section a week. We argue it till the paragraph runs out. You don’t get to say *mystery* to get out of a corner, and I don’t get to say *patriarchy* to get out of one.”
“Fair.”

“Fair is a word for losers. Okay.” She holds her copy out at arm’s length and reads the first sentence in a casting director’s voice — flat, fast, nasal, a woman at the end of a long day of hallways and folding chairs:
“*The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God.*” She lowers the book. “SEEKING: everyone. Any age, any type. Must want God. Non-union okay. No pay.”

“Here’s how every script I’ve ever opened starts,” Skye says, still in it. “Page one, before anything: what does she want. Not what she says. What she *wants*. The want is the character. Two people want different things and you’ve got a scene. In *Sweetwater* I wanted out of Sweetwater for three seasons. You can play that. You can play that drunk.” She turns the book around and taps the sentence. “This gives every character in the world the *same* want. That’s not a character. That’s a casting call.”
She sets the book down, and the casting director goes with it.

“Okay. Here’s my real problem.” She pulls one knee up under the silk and wraps her arms around it, and the slit does what slits do, and either she doesn’t notice or she does it on purpose; with her he has never been able to tell. “Wanting a father up there is what every kid on earth does. That’s exactly why I don’t trust it. You want somebody to be watching, so you decide somebody is.” She looks out the window. “I wanted a lot of things when I was four that didn’t come back.”

She turns back to him. “And I know exactly how much a person can make herself feel if she needs to. It’s my job. Season two, I cried for a dead dog. The dog was a stuffed animal on a stick, and the guy holding the stick was eating a burrito, and I cried real tears for four takes and on the fourth one I meant it. A feeling isn’t proof of anything. I can make one before lunch.”
He opens his mouth and she holds up one finger.

“No. Wait. I’m not done.” She lets go of her knee and puts the foot back down on the concrete. “And this is the one I actually lose sleep over. Whatever I want, you get to say what I *really* want is God. A cheeseburger: God. You: God.” She doesn’t blink on it. “Winning this: God. You can’t lose. That’s how I know it’s a trick.”

She sits back and hooks her bare heels on the rung of the chair and waits, the pen cap in her teeth, and one of the pins has started to work loose at the back of her hair, so that a dark piece of it has come down against her neck. She doesn’t fix it. The window light is on one side of her face and the rest of the shop is on the other, and all of it is waiting for him.

It’s good. It’s the objection he’d make himself if he were sitting on her side of the table, and she has made it in silk in under five minutes without a glance at the book. Jack looks at the window while he finds a place to start. She’s right about the dog; he believes her about the dog. He has knelt on a basement floor on Glenwood Avenue and felt nothing at all, and he has felt a great deal on nights when he had no business feeling anything, and neither one proved a thing either way. That isn’t where he’d start.

choices.text: *The argument from desire: nobody’s born hungry in a world without food.*
response: “You don’t get a want with nothing on the other end of it,” he says. “Thirst, there’s water. Hunger, there’s food. Lonely, there’s people. Lewis has it somewhere — a baby gets hungry, and it turns out there’s such a thing as food. So if there’s a want nothing in this world fills, maybe you were made for somewhere else too.”
“People want to fly.”
“And there’s air.” He shrugs. “Took us a while to work out what to do with it.”
She uncaps the yellow highlighter, considers the line, caps it again, and uncaps the green.

choices.text: *It doesn’t say the cheeseburger is secretly God. It says the cheeseburger doesn’t finish the job.*
response: “It doesn’t say the cheeseburger’s secretly God,” he says. “Read the next sentence. It says there’s a thing you never stop looking for. You eat the cheeseburger and you want the next thing. You win this, you’ll want the next one. It isn’t saying you want God *instead*. It’s saying nothing you get is the end of wanting.”
“That’s worse,” she says. “That’s a hamster wheel.”
“It’s a hamster wheel if there’s nothing at the end of it. That’s the bet.”
She opens her mouth, and shuts it, and goes back to the paragraph and reads the second sentence again to herself, her lips moving a little on the words.

choices.text: “You’ve read a script where everyone wants the same thing. It’s called a love story.”
response: “You’ve read a script where everyone wants the same thing,” he says. “It’s called a love story.”
She laughs, loud, head down over the binder, the diamonds swinging.

“Yes, *and* — the critics hate it, and it makes a fortune every single time, and nobody in the audience ever asks for their money back.” She says it into the binder, and doesn’t look up until he’s stopped grinning.

choices.text: “You’re right that wanting doesn’t prove it. The book doesn’t say it does. It says it’s where you start looking.”
response: “You’re right that wanting doesn’t prove it,” he says. “The book doesn’t say it does. It says it’s where you start looking.”
She looks at him past the end of the point, and goes on looking.
“Okay,” she says. “That’s fair. I hate fair.”
She writes START LOOKING across the top of the page and draws a box around it.

body: She skips nothing. Twenty-eight goes by with a yellow line under it — people have always gone looking, in prayers and sacrifices and rituals, everywhere, and she seems to find that fair — and then twenty-nine, where the bond can be forgotten, overlooked, even rejected outright, and she sits up very straight and becomes an agent’s assistant reading the passes off a legal pad, in a bright Valley voice that has broken a great deal of bad news to a great many people.

“Okay, so, the notes are in. *Revolt against evil in the world* — they’re passing. *Religious ignorance or indifference* — passing. *The cares and riches of this world* — they loved it, they’re passing. *The scandal of bad example on the part of believers.* Pass. *Currents of thought hostile to religion*, pass, and finally, *that attitude of sinful man which makes him hide from God out of fear and flee his call.* So that’s a pass from Adam. From the bushes.” She looks up at him over the imaginary pad. “Number four. ‘The scandal of bad example on the part of believers.’ I’d like you to sit with that.”

He sits with it. There is plenty to sit with: the bishops, the files in Boston, the word *moved*, the parishes that had to sell the school to pay for it. She isn’t wrong to make him sit, and she lets the Valley go.

“It’s honest,” she says. “I’ll give it that. It lists *you*. Most places don’t put themselves on the list of reasons people leave.” She runs the capped pen down the paragraph. “That’s —” Jack says. “Let me finish,” she says. “Look at it. Every reason on here is something wrong with the one who leaves. Angry. Ignorant. Too rich. Scandalized. Reading the wrong books. Hiding. Nowhere does it say *some people looked, and nobody was there.*” She taps the page. “You’ve written the reviews before the show opens.”
She leans in on her elbows over the binder, close enough that he can see where the powder stops at her hairline. She smells like something expensive and a little like the rain on the window.

“I went to Mass with you. Two Sundays and a Tuesday with a candle in each hand. I knelt when you knelt. I learned the words. I listened, and I mean *listened*, the way I listen to a scene partner when I don’t know what he’s going to do. I’d have taken anything. A feeling. A coincidence. A parking space.” Her voice doesn’t go up. “I’m not hiding in the bushes. I’m standing in the middle of the yard, waving. If he never stops calling, why can’t I hear him?”

There are nights on his step, third down from four, when Jack can’t hear anything either, when what he says goes up the stairwell as far as the tube light and no farther. He has had those nights since he was confirmed. He goes anyway, those nights. He kneels and says it into the dark and goes to bed. That’s the only answer he has ever had for it, and it isn’t an argument, and she would know that. She has walked straight to the best argument there is, and she found it in a list.

choices.text: *A God who showed up like a billboard wouldn’t leave you free to say no.*
response: “If he showed up like a billboard,” Jack says, “you couldn’t say no to him. You’d believe in him the way you believe in gravity. And you’d love him the way you love gravity.” He leans back. “Pascal says there’s enough light for anybody who wants to see, and enough dark for anybody who doesn’t. The dark’s the door. He leaves it open both ways.”
“That’s a very convenient amount of dark.”
“It’s the amount you’d need to be free.”
“A door isn’t a call.”
“A call you can’t say no to is an order.”
“Maybe I’d like an order.” She doesn’t smile. “I take direction beautifully.”

choices.text: *Waving in the middle of the yard is looking. The book’s bet is that the looking is him.*
response: “Read the start of thirty,” he says. “He never stops calling everybody to look for him. You’re standing in the yard waving. That’s looking. You think you’re waving at nobody. The book thinks the wave is the answer. You said you’d have taken a parking space. You sat in a pew, listening. The book would say somebody kept you there.”
She opens her mouth, and there’s nothing ready in it. She looks at the strap of the gown, at the window, at him.
“Say the part about the waving again,” she says. “Slower.”

choices.text: “It’s written from the inside. You’re right. It can’t tell you what it looks like from the yard.”
response: “It’s written from the inside,” he says. “You’re right. It can’t tell you what it looks like from the yard.” And then, because it’s true and she ought to have it: “There are nights I can’t hear him either.”
“What do you do? Those nights.”
“Go anyway.”
She looks at him. She nods, slowly, more than once.
“Thank you,” she says.
She writes FROM THE YARD on a yellow Post-it and sticks it inside the front pocket of the binder, and smooths it down with the side of her thumb.

choices.text: “Adam hid in a bush. You’d have asked for a better bush.”
response: “Adam hid in a bush,” he says. “You’d have asked for a better bush.”

“I’d have asked for *lighting*.” It gets as far as her eyes and no farther. “And a piece of tape on the floor, so he’d know where to find me. That’s my point, Costigan. I’m on my mark. I’ve been on it since January.”
She waits to see whether he has anything under the joke. When he doesn’t, she turns the page.

choices.text: *“You weren’t in the yard. The night we met you told me you sit still and listen for something, and you don’t expect anybody to answer.”*
response: “You weren’t in the yard,” he says. “The night we met, you told me you sit still and listen for something. And you don’t expect anybody to answer.”
It lands. She goes still in her chair with the pen stopped above the page.
When she speaks it’s level. “That’s a good one.” She looks at him. “That’s going in the binder.”
She writes it down, and doesn’t hurry, and the diamonds at her ears catch the window every time her head moves.

body: Thirty is short. She reads it through to herself, and gets to the bottom, and something in it makes her push her chair back and stand up, barefoot on the concrete, in the gown.
Every head in Low Tide comes round. She lifts one hand, palm out, over the bike path, a bishop on a balcony above a square full of people.

“*Augustine*,” she announces. “Of Hippo. Picture him. A Shakespearean Hippo.” She draws herself up, and in a voice from the back of a very old theater, rolling every r there is, she tells Las Olas: “*You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.*”
Behind the counter the barista laughs and claps twice, with the milk jug still in one hand.

While Skye holds the pose, Jack’s hand goes to the breast pocket of the Carhartt. It finds the canvas, and under the canvas the cellophane, and the hard corner of the pack, the Reds, shut. It’s day twenty-two. His thumb runs along the edge of the cellophane to where the tear strip starts, and stops there. The pack stays sealed. He takes the hand back down and picks up his pen.
She bows to the barista, very low, one hand on her heart, and sits. She pulls the silk straight over her knee and puts both hands on the binder, and the bishop is gone.

“I’ve been restless since I was eleven,” she says. “At eleven I booked a cereal commercial and wanted a series. At thirteen I wanted my own show. At sixteen I had it. I called it ambition. My mother called it a career. Every time I got the thing, I wanted the next thing before I’d finished being happy about the first one. I booked *Sweetwater* and cried in the parking garage, and by the time I got to the car I was thinking about what I’d do after it got canceled. I’ve never been where I was.” She turns the book around to face him. “And you’re telling me it’s somebody calling. That’s the most romantic line in the book, and I don’t trust it, because it’s the line every man has ever used on me. *What you’re really looking for is me.*”

body.text: She keeps her eyes on him. “You told me at the Starlite it’s true first. Show me where it’s true first, and not just the line.”

body: Outside, the light on the bike path has started to go long and yellow, and the bikes going by throw long shadows in across the concrete floor. She waits for him, with her chin up and the pen capped in her fist.

It’s a fair hit, and he takes it. In January he told her he loved her, before she ever said it, and he meant it, and four weeks later he was standing at the bottom of her steps. He knows what a line sounds like from her side of the table. He isn’t the one who gets to tell her this isn’t one.

And still. He has read the thing she’s quoting, all thirteen books of it, the summer before Marisol, on the back porch on Glenwood with a pencil — Augustine in a garden in Milan, wrecked, on the ground under a fig tree, and a child’s voice from the house next door singing some game, *take it and read, take it and read*, and him getting up off the ground and doing it. In that garden there wasn’t anybody trying to get anything off anybody.

choices.text: *Augustine isn’t a guy at a bar. He tried everything else first and wrote every one of them down.*
choices.key: When Skye called Augustine’s restless heart a line, you told her he’d tried everything else first and written it all down.
response: “Augustine isn’t a guy at a bar,” Jack says. “He tried everything else first. The girlfriend, the career, the Manichees, the pears. And he wrote every one of them down. He’s confessing it. Thirteen books of *I tried that too.*”
“The pears?”

“He stole some pears off a tree when he was sixteen. Didn’t want them. Threw them to the pigs. He wrote pages about why. You asked what the character wants — he spent his life on that one question, and he wrote down every wrong answer he gave it.”
She stares at him. “That is the most Catholic sentence anyone has ever said to me, and I’ve been to a christening.”
She writes 13 BOOKS in the margin and underlines it, hard enough to come through on the next page.

choices.text: *The difference between a line and the truth is whether the one saying it needs you to believe it.*
choices.key: When Skye called Augustine’s restless heart a line, you told her a line is something the speaker needs you to believe, and that God doesn’t need it.
response: “The difference between a line and the truth,” he says, “is whether the one saying it needs you to believe it. Every man who used that on you needed something from you. He doesn’t. He’ll be there if you say no. He’ll be there if you walk out of here and never open the book again. A line wants something back, and it wants it tonight.”
It takes her a long time.
“That’s a director’s note,” she says at last. “I hate it when they’re right.”
She says it straight at him, and lets him watch her think about it.

choices.text: “I can’t prove the restlessness is him. I believe it. That’s the difference between us, and it’s the whole thing.”
choices.key: When Skye called Augustine’s restless heart a line, you told her you couldn’t prove it, only believe it, and that this was the difference between you.
response: “I can’t prove the restlessness is him,” he says. “I believe it. That’s the difference between us. That’s all of it.”
She looks at him, and for a moment it’s her face on the porch on Del Playa — and then it’s gone, and she’s here.
“Yeah,” she says. “It is.”
She turns it over. “For the record, that’s the first thing you’ve said all afternoon I can’t argue with. I’m going to try anyway. Next week. At length.”
She doesn’t write that one down.

choices.text: *“You answer every call with ‘hi’ and you don’t know who it’s for.”*
choices.key: When Skye called Augustine’s restless heart a line, you threw her own Lent back at her — that she says hi to every call and doesn’t know who for.
response: “You answer every call with *hi*,” he says. “And you don’t know who it’s for.”
She goes absolutely still.
“I told you that in my car.”
“I know.”
“Okay.”
It won the point. It was hers, and she gave it to him in her own car, and he can’t give it back.
She bends over the book and writes something in the margin, small, that he can’t read upside down, and when she’s finished she leaves her hand lying over it.

choices.text: “If it’s a line, it’s the oldest one in the book. Sixteen hundred years, and it’s still working.”
choices.key: When Skye called Augustine’s restless heart a line, you told her that if it was a line, it was sixteen hundred years old and still working.
response: “If it’s a line,” he says, “it’s the oldest one in the book. Sixteen hundred years, and it’s still working.”
“So is *I’ll call you*.” She lets that sit just long enough to be sure he heard it. “Longevity isn’t truth, Costigan. It’s distribution.”
She drinks some of her coffee and looks at him over the cup, and waits to see if he has anything else, and he hasn’t.

s07d.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:40 PM · LOW TIDE — BRING PROOFS
body: The sun has got down under the edge of the cloud and in at the long window, and the wet bike path outside has gone to gold, and paragraph thirty is done. She sits back. She looks at the open book, and at him, and at the book, a long, level look over the top of it.

body.text: Skye closes the book on her pen and looks at him over it. “Draw,” she says. “I hate draws. Draws are what you get when both actors are good and the director’s asleep.” She opens the back cover and writes DRAW inside it, small, in pink, and regards it with distaste.
Skye closes the book on her pen and looks at him over it. “Fine,” she says. “Chapter One, Roman numeral one, to you. Don’t get used to it.”
“The thirteen books. That was good.”
“The thing about who needs the line. I’ll be turning that over till Friday.”
“And the other thing.”
“And then you gave me the last one. I resent that more.”
“The billboard. That one’s going in green.”
“The waving. I’m going to be annoyed about the waving all week.”

Skye closes the book on her pen, and opens it again at the back. “Mine,” she says. “Write it down.” He doesn’t, so she does: inside the back cover, in green, SKYE 1 — COSTIGAN 0. “Green is for good lines,” she says, and blows on it.
“That was a cheap shot,” she says. “It was also a good one. I’m keeping it.”

body: She takes the receipt out of the gutter and moves it on, past the end of thirty, and opens the book flat and turns it to him with one finger under the heading. “‘Ways of Coming to Know God.’ Next Wednesday. Bring proofs. You’ve got a few; I looked ahead. That isn’t cheating, that’s the table of contents.”

She packs up — the binder, the three highlighters in their row, the worksheet folder — and under the table her feet find the gold heels and step into them, straps loose. She stands, and goes out first, down the length of the shop, in silk, past the counter and the racks and the surfers, and doesn’t look back. At the door she puts one hand on the doorframe and does up the buckles, the left and then the right, and goes out onto Las Olas. The barista watches her go. So do both surfers. So, as far as Jack can tell, does the bike path.
She never touched him — not his hand, not his sleeve; even the coffee was set down, not handed.
The barista comes over with a rag for the table and stands holding it, looking at the door. “Okay, is she, like —” She stops. “Is that *somebody*?”
“She’s in my oceanography class,” Jack says.

The barista looks at him, and at the chipped mug, and at the sugar packets still laid out on the plywood in their line, and at the bobby pin lying beside them that came out of Skye’s hair somewhere around paragraph twenty-seven, and wipes around all of it.

Once the barista is back behind the counter he finishes the cold coffee. He opens his own book to thirty-one. The stranger’s pencil stops at thirty, at the *yes*; from thirty-one on the pages are clean.

When he comes out onto the sidewalk with his book under his arm, the wet street has gone orange, and the cold is coming up off it. Up Ocean Road, the light might be on in Father Osei’s office. Back at Delgado there’s 412, and Theo, and the coffee can.
