s08o.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR, FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — A PILGRIMAGE
body: The light is on. It’s the only one along the office wing, a yellow square low on the side of St. Brendan’s, and from the courtyard Jack can hear the record through the glass: two guitars chasing each other over a bright little horn line, turned down low for the neighbors.

Father Osei opens the door before the second knock, in his black shirt with the collar out of it and the sleeves turned back, his reading glasses on their cord. “Jack. Come. Sit. You are not kneeling tonight, so you may have the good chair.”

The good chair has a cushion. The office is the size of a parking space, books on the floor in towers, the turntable on the filing cabinet with the record going round, and on the desk a chessboard with a game half played on it, which Osei has been playing by mail since Advent with a retired Jesuit in Sacramento who takes eleven days a move. Osei sits on the corner of the desk with his bad leg out straight.
“So,” he says. “What is good enough to bring you up Ocean Road in the dark?”

“Is it all right,” Jack says, “if I meet Skye on Wednesdays to argue about the Catechism?” And because that isn’t really the question, he tells it from the start: the paperback on his notebook on Tuesday, from the beginning, in order; Wednesdays at four at Low Tide; today, paragraphs twenty-seven to thirty; and the gown.

Osei laughs. He doesn’t try to hide it; he takes the glasses off and laughs till he has to wipe one eye with his thumb. “Black silk,” he says. “At four o’clock. On a Wednesday.” He puts the glasses back on. “Read the page.”

Jack tells him the rest. That he told Lena first, Tuesday afternoon, on the empty stage at Sandoval, before anybody else could. That she asked him three questions and gave him one condition: if Skye ever makes a move, it stops — the coffees, the book, all of it. That he promised.
“And will you keep it?”
“Yes.”
“Keep it to the letter,” Osei says. “And keep it in the open. Not in your pocket like a stone you turn over when nobody is looking. Lena should never have to ask you whether you are keeping it.”
He lets the record play a little.
“And you,” he says. “What do you want from these Wednesdays?”
Jack has to think about it. “I want it to be good for her,” he says. “Whatever she ends up thinking. I want her to come out of it better off than she went in.”

“To want the good of another person for her own sake,” Osei says. “Thomas has a word for that, and you know the word, and it is allowed you, even for her. Especially for her.” He tilts his head at the record; it has gone into a long guitar break. “Only make sure it is her good you are wanting, and not the good of being the man across the table from her.”
“And the girl,” Osei says. “What do you think she wants?”
“To win.”

“Perhaps. She is an actress; she likes to win. But I think she wants to understand what took you from her.” He spreads his hands. “That is not an attack. It is a pilgrimage, though I would not use the word to her face.”
“She picked the place. A surf shop. Four in the afternoon. There’s a window on the bike path.”
Osei nods slowly. “She chose the hour. She chose it well. That tells you something about her you should not forget.”

He gets up off the desk. “Now we pray. Short. For her, and for Lena, and for you, who will need it most on Wednesdays.” He says the Hail Mary in his slow, exact English, and Jack takes the second half with him, and under it the guitars go on chasing each other on the filing cabinet.
“Ɛyɛ,” Osei says, at the end, and sits back down. “And tomorrow, tell Lena about the gown. All of it. Tell her the funny part first.”

choices.text: “What if she’s right about something?”
response: “What if she’s right about something?”
“Then you will have learned something,” Osei says. “God is not afraid of a good argument. Only of a dishonest one. If she shows you something true, it is his already. Take it home.”
He gets up and lifts the needle at the end of the side, and turns the record over, and sets it down again on the other side, carefully, with his little finger crooked.

choices.text: “I still love her. That didn’t stop when I left.”
response: “I still love her,” Jack says. “That didn’t stop when I left.”
Osei lets it sit a moment.
“No. It does not,” he says. “It is not a sin to have loved somebody, Jack. It is only a sin to lie about which way you are facing.”
He folds his hands on the desk, one thumb over the other, and waits there until Jack can look at him again.

choices.text: *Listen to the record to the end.*
response: Jack doesn’t say anything else, and Osei lets him not. They sit and listen to the side play out, the guitars and the little horns and a man singing in a language Jack doesn’t have about something that is obviously going very well, till the needle runs in toward the label and starts to hiss.
Osei gets up and lifts it.
“Wednesdays, then,” he says, and smiles at him.

s08t.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE WHOLE THING
body: Theo is sitting cross-legged on his bed with the coffee can from Sunday’s Oscar pool between his knees and the money laid out on the bedspread in piles: ones, fives, a twenty somebody is going to want change for, and an IOU from Margot on a strip of notebook paper that says *Sound Mixing — UNDER PROTEST*. He is counting it for the third time. He likes counting money. He says it’s the only honest thing in Hollywood.
“You’ve got a face,” he says, to the money. “Sit. Say it. I’m on the fives.”

Jack sits on his own bed under the crucifix and says it. That Skye came back to Oceanography last Thursday. That on Tuesday she put a paperback Catechism down on his notebook and said she wanted to read it with him, from the beginning, in order, one section at a time, till one of them talked the other one round. Wednesdays at four, at an old surf shop on Las Olas with a window on the bike path. That today was the first one, and that she came in a gown — a real one, black, to the floor — and corrected his tide math in it, and then took him apart on the desire for God for an hour and a half.
Theo has stopped counting at *came back*. He has a five in his hand, up in the air, and it hangs there through the rest of it.
“She came back,” he says. “To *class*.” He puts the five down on the wrong pile. “And she’s going to read the *Catechism*. The whole thing. Front to back.”
“Every word.”
“What was the first thing she said?”
“‘Yes. It’s a strategy.’”
Theo laughs, one short bark at the ceiling. “Of course it is. And you looked.”
“I looked.”
“Good. If you’d told me you didn’t, I’d have had you committed.” He picks the five back up off the wrong pile. “Who won?”

body.text: “Nobody. She called it a draw and wrote it in the back of her book like a parking ticket.”
“Me. On points. Narrowly.”
“Her. On points. She wrote it down in green.”

body: Theo comes up onto his knees on the bed and frames it with his hands. “A girl, a gown, and two thousand eight hundred paragraphs.” He holds it there. “Sundance. Midnight screening. They’d have to carry people out.”
He sits back on his heels, and the bit goes out of him, and he looks down at the money. He picks up Margot’s IOU and reads it and puts it back on its own pile.

“She finishes things,” he says. “When she was fourteen a director told her she didn’t understand her own character, and she went home and read all of Stanislavski in a weekend to prove him wrong. All of it. Came back Monday and took him apart in front of the crew.” He knocks a stack of ones straight on his knee. “She won. He cast her again the next year. He said he’d never been so scared of a fourteen-year-old.” He sets the ones down. “She doesn’t get bored. Other people get bored. She gets to the end.”
Down the hall somebody’s door bangs and a girl laughs and is gone.
“Be careful with her, Costigan,” Theo says, still counting. “Not for you.”
He counts four ones and stops.
“Does Lena know?”
“Yesterday. Before anybody.”
“Good.” He goes back to the ones.

Eventually he puts the lid half on the can and pats it. “Tomorrow night,” he says, “this is the only licensed bookmaker in Sandoval Hall. Hale at three to one, Broussard odds-on. I’m being generous to Hale out of pity. Do you want a piece?”
“No.”
“Father Jack. Of course you don’t.” He writes something on the back of Margot’s IOU. “I’ll put you down for moral support.”

He pushes the can back against the wall with his foot. “And next week she’ll have something new. She never wears the same thing twice in front of the same audience. She didn’t when we were eleven.” He lies back on his elbows and looks at the ceiling.

choices.text: “I’m not going to hurt her again.”
response: “I’m not going to hurt her again.”
Theo looks at him across the room.
“You will,” he says. “Do it honestly.”
He fits the plastic lid back on the coffee can and presses it down all the way round with his thumb.

choices.text: “It was a gown, Theo. An actual gown.”
response: “It was a gown, Theo. An actual gown.”
“Of course it was. Which one?”
Jack tells him: black, silk, no back to speak of, a slit, straps like bootlaces, the diamonds.

“Season two,” Theo says. “The premiere. She hated the shoes.” He lies back among the fives and looks at the ceiling. “At a *surf shop*.” He thinks about it. “It’s the only dress she ever got to keep.” He puts one hand over his eyes and leaves it there.

choices.text: “I want to understand it too. What I did.”
response: “I want to understand it too,” Jack says. “What I did.”
Theo, for once, has no line. He looks at Jack, and then he pats the mattress beside him, twice.

Jack crosses the room and sits on the edge of Theo’s bed among the piles of money, and after a minute Theo reaches over and turns off the lamp, and the two of them sit there with the light from the hall coming in under the door.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 11:00 AM · MORRO HALL 1100 — SPRING TIDES
body: The rain blew through in the night and took the cloud with it, and the sky over the lagoon is a hard, scrubbed blue that shows in every puddle on the Morro steps. Somebody has taped a flyer to the glass of the left-hand door at eye height.

body.title: Flyer, Morro Hall door
body.text:
THE MARISOL FORUM · TONIGHT · 7 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1
“THAT ONE CAN BE GOOD WITHOUT GOD”
PROF. ADRIAN HALE, PROPOSING · MS. MAGDALENA BROUSSARD, OPPOSING
Free · Cards at the door

body: Skye is on the steps ahead of him, bag on her shoulder. She goes past the flyer and in through the door without slowing, and he catches the door on its swing and follows her up the tiers.
She’s in the back row under the exit sign by the time he gets there, her bag on the floor on her own side.
“Hi,” she says.
Jeans, the navy sweater, her hair loose today and still damp at the ends from a shower, a ballpoint.

Down at the bottom of the room Fenner has the sun and the moon on their string again and is very happy to see them. The spring tide is Monday and Tuesday, he tells the room — sun and moon pulling the same way, the highest highs of the month, the lowest lows. “Go down to the wharf at the low and look at the pilings. All the way down to the mud. There are things living on those pilings you would not believe, and I am going to ask.”
“He isn’t going to ask,” Skye says, writing PILINGS in the margin and boxing it.
“He might.”
“He has never followed up on anything. It’s what I like about him.”

For an hour and a quarter they take down Fenner’s tides side by side. She asks him one thing about the lunar day — why the tide comes fifty minutes later every day instead of at the same time like a decent person — and he tells her, and she writes it down and puts a small check beside it in the margin.

At a quarter past twelve the room comes apart down the tiers in zippers and backpacks, and Jack leans down for his bag under the seat. When he comes back up there is a yellow square on his open notebook, pressed flat with a thumb, squarely in the middle of his tides.

body.title: Post-it, yellow
body.text: ¶31. PROOFS. WED.

body: Her seat is folded up. The side door at the bottom of the tiers is still swinging. He peels the square off the notebook and sticks it inside the front cover of his four-dollar Catechism, where the stranger who owned it before him never wrote a word.

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 5:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 217 — DRESSED FOR WAR
body: At one o’clock PHIL 109H was called off by a note on the door of 302, in fountain pen, in the tall hand that leans backward:

body.title: Note, Hollis 302
body.text: No seminar. Miss Broussard is excused the burden of being taught today; the rest of you are excused the burden of me. —A.H.

body: Caleb read it three times with his nose nearly on the glass. “Dude,” he said, “he’s *nervous*,” and went off down the Hollis stairs at a jog, as though somebody ought to be told.

Now the door of 217 stands open to the corridor and every light in the room is on: the overhead, both desk lamps, the string of chili-pepper lights round Laney’s mirror. In the middle of it Lena sits on her desk chair, turned backward to the hall with her arms folded along the top of it, being got ready.

“For a war,” Laney says, around a mouthful of bobby pins. She has Lena’s hair in one fist and a rat-tail comb in the other. “Not a date. On a date you want them to *wonder*. At a war you want them to *know*.”

The black blazer hangs on the back of the closet door, pressed, a dry cleaner’s tag still pinned to the sleeve. Lena is in a white blouse buttoned to the collar with her grandmother’s medal outside it, where anybody in Sandoval will be able to see it from the back row, and a pair of black flats waits under the bed, side by side, the ones she can stand in for an hour. Laney spits the pins into her palm one at a time and puts them where they go, and then holds up a single strand of pearls from the clutter on her desk, and lays them across her own collarbone, and raises her eyebrows at Lena over the top of her head.
“I am not wearing pearls,” Lena says, “to argue with an atheist.”
“Pearls are a *threat*.”
Lena looks at the pearls for about as long as it takes Laney to fasten them on her.

Margot is cross-legged on Laney’s bed among the discarded options — a red scarf, a gray cardigan, a belt with no known purpose — with a steno pad on her knee and a laminated badge clipped to the collar of her shirt: THE MARISOL TIDE · PRESS. She uncaps a pen.
“I need one quote from the opposition before the event,” she says. “For color. Are you going to win?”
“Yes.”
“Good. That’s the headline.” Margot writes it down. “I drafted the other headline too, in case. It has the word *valiant* in it. I would hate to waste *valiant* on a Thursday.”

Jack stands in the doorway with his hands in his pockets. Laney has not invited him in and has not needed to say so. Lena’s face is made up for the hall — whatever was under her eyes on Monday has been painted out, and her mouth is a dark red he has never seen on it — and she looks back at him over the top of the chair as steady as a picture of herself.

“Lena told me about Wednesdays,” Laney says, pushing a pin home over Lena’s left ear. “And I want to say one thing about that girl, sugar, and it is that I *like* her. I have always liked her. Which is exactly why I would drown her in the lagoon with my own two hands and then send the most *beautiful* —”
“Laney.”

Lena doesn’t raise it, and doesn’t turn round. Laney stops. She puts the next pin in where it goes and says nothing else, and for a little while the only sound in 217 is the hiss of the hairspray going on in a long careful cloud. Lena looks at Margot over the back of the chair.
“Next question.”
“I only had the one,” Margot says.

Five minutes later Lena comes out into the corridor in her stocking feet, the pearls and the medal lying together at her collar, and Laney pushes the door half shut behind her and starts humming something inside with a key change in it. The tube light down the hall at the stairwell end buzzes and holds.
“How was Wednesday?” Lena asks. Low; just for the corridor.
“We argued the first four paragraphs,” he says.

body.text: “A draw. She hates draws.”
“I took it. She says not to get used to it.”
“She took it. She wrote it in the back of her book.”

body: “She wore a gown. To a coffee shop. On purpose.”
For one second Lena’s face does nothing at all.
“Did she keep her hands to herself?”
“Yes.”
“Then it’s Wednesday.”

There is no joke in it anywhere, and no edge either; she says it like the time of the next bus. She turns it back to tonight before he can add a word. “My cards are in the left pocket of the blazer. If my hand goes there, I’m losing, and I don’t want to see your face know it.”
“What should it do?”
“Ohio,” she says. “Flat. No weather.”

She goes up on her toes in her stocking feet and kisses him, quick, for luck. The lipstick is waxy and tastes faintly of raspberries and of money, and her hand is cold on the side of his face, and then she’s down again.
From inside 217, through the gap in the door, Laney: “*Lipstick!* That mouth is for the *public*!”

Lena wipes the corner of his mouth with the side of her thumb, frowning at it, and doesn’t tell him where to sit. She goes back in. Through the gap before the door closes he sees her sit down again on the backward chair with her chin up, and shut her eyes, and hold her face still for Laney’s brush.

s11.slug: THURSDAY · 7:00 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — THE MOTION
body: Two days ago this hall was empty seats going up into the dark and one worklight. Tonight the house lights are all the way up, nearly every orange seat has somebody in it, and a few latecomers are standing along the back wall under the fire marshal’s sign. On the stage, the two lecterns, the table in the middle, and on the table now a pitcher of water and two glasses.
Jack has the third row, on the aisle. Laney has the seat beside him, in a fire-engine dress, because, she says, somebody in this row has to be visible from the stage without binoculars.

At the left-hand end of the table Lena sits in the black blazer with the pearls and the medal at her collar and her hands folded on the bare table. At the right-hand end Hale sits with one long leg crossed over the other, reading a paperback of *Brideshead Revisited* with every appearance of enjoying it.
From two rows back comes the rattle of the Oscar coffee can. “Broussard, heavy,” Theo is telling the sophomore beside him, and takes the sophomore’s five.

The Dean of Humanities comes to the side of the stage, a small woman in her sixties in a plum suit with reading glasses on a beaded chain, and explains the cards. Everyone was handed three at the door, out of the box Evan Marsh is still holding there — white for the motion, red against, gray for not yet — and dropped a slip in a shoebox on the way in. That’s where the evening starts. At the end, a card in a box: that’s where it finishes. “The winner,” she says, “is not whoever has the room. It’s whoever moves it.” She reads from an index card. “For the motion, two hundred and eleven. Against, ninety-eight. Undecided, sixty-three.”
In the front row Caleb Hargrove, in a clip-on tie, hugs Hale’s book to his chest; beside him Yusuf goes on eating sunflower seeds out of a paper bag, one at a time, spitting the shells into his hand.
“We’re *losing*,” Laney says.
“That’s the point.”
The Dean comes along the table to Hale with a little clip-on microphone held out on her palm, the cord trailing. He looks down at it, and up at her, kindly.
“I have been heard in worse rooms without help.”
The hall laughs and he hasn’t started yet. He doesn’t go to his lectern. He comes round in front of it with his hands behind his back, and walks.

“Miss Broussard,” he says, “will tell you that *ought* is a word with a debt in it. I propose to save her the trouble. She’s right. When I say you ought to ring your mother, I mean you owe her a phone call. Every *ought* has the shape of an IOU. I have spent thirty years trying to get that shape out of the language with a crowbar, and I can’t. Debts have creditors. I grant it.”

He turns on his heel. “I deny one thing only — that the creditor has to be invisible. Look along your row. The creditors are in this room. The girl who lent you her notes. The man who held the door. The mother you will not, in fact, ring on Sunday. What we owe, we owe to each other; an American called Scanlon wrote a large and very good book to that effect, and I commend to you its title, which is the argument. And there is a good man in the third row.” He doesn’t look at the third row. “There is always a good man in the third row. He visits his mother. He keeps his word. He does not need a ghost standing behind him with a ledger to make him do it, and it is insulting — if the Dean will forgive me, it is *bollocks* — to tell him he does.”

Across the aisle Jack sees Clare Dominguez in among the Newman band kids lift one hand to somebody halfway up the house, and halfway up the house Kevin, alone in the middle of a row, lifts one back. A raised hand each way across the hall, and both hands go back down.

body.text: “Goodness isn’t handed down from a mountain,” Hale says. “It grows up out of what we are, the way a root’s good is to take up water. Philippa Foot taught me that, and Miss Broussard granted it at my own table a week ago Monday — Miss Broussard’s wolf. A wolf that won’t hunt with the pack is a bad wolf, and nobody had to carve the pack a commandment.”
body.else: “Goodness isn’t handed down from a mountain,” Hale says. “It grows up out of what we are, the way a root’s good is to take up water. Philippa Foot taught me that, and Miss Broussard fought me for it at my own table a week ago Monday, and will tell you, I expect, that she won. Nobody had to carve the roots a commandment.”

body: He stops, dead center, and rocks once on his heels. “I have been told I am the Church’s most useful atheist. I have never been paid.”

The room adores him. At the back by the doors, in his collar, Father Osei stands with his arms folded and his head on one side, and Margot, on her way past him to the press table and the *Tide*’s photographer, gives him a small white card out of her badge pocket. He reads it, and puts it away inside his jacket.

Jack has watched Hale do this since October, and waits for Euthyphro, the knife Hale always reaches for. It doesn’t come. Hale goes past the place where it ought to be twice and leaves it in the drawer.
“So vote for the motion, or don’t,” Hale says, coming back to his chair. “I shall sit down in a moment, and then Miss Broussard has the floor, and I have the rest of my life.”

The laugh is the biggest of the night. At her end of the table Lena laughs with everybody else, honestly, with her head back, and then picks up her programme and a pencil and writes something across the top of it.

s11a.slug: THURSDAY · 7:25 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — THE FIRST TWO MINUTES
body: The Dean comes back to the side of the stage and takes her glasses off their chain and puts them on, and reads off nothing.
“Miss Broussard has the floor.”

Lena stands up. She leaves the programme on the table and the cards in her pocket. She doesn’t go to her own lectern; she walks across the front of the stage in her flats, past the water pitcher, to Hale’s side, and stops on the board in front of his lectern, and when she shifts her weight it creaks. Hale, in his chair, watches her take his ground with one eyebrow up. Jack would bet he and the girl standing on it are the only two people in Sandoval who knew that board was going to say something.
He looks at the clock on the wall over the stage as she opens her mouth. The second hand is on the twelve.

body.text: She starts with the debt. “Professor Hale has just told you that you owe each other everything,” she says. “He’s right. I want to ask him one question about the word.” Three days of saying it to a fire door, and tonight for the first time it’s in the right tense.

“Professor Hale would like me to play the woman who thinks you’re all going to hell,” she says. “I’ve read the script. I’m not taking the role.” The laugh comes, surprised, and she waits it out. “He’s told you that you owe each other everything. He’s right. I want to ask him one question about the word.”

She turns her back on the hall and says her first sentence to Hale, in his chair, to his face. “You’ve just told them they owe each other everything. You’re right. I want to ask you one question about the word.” And only then turns round to the hall.

“Professor Hale has just told you that you owe each other everything. He’s right,” she says. “And the word he used for it was *owes*.” She stops on it. She leaves the silence standing on the stage beside her and doesn’t touch it, and the hall leans in toward it, row by row, to see what she’s going to put in it.

body: Jack stops hearing it as a speech after that. He watches the room. He has watched her turn a room from across an oak table since August; this is the first time he has watched it from the outside. It doesn’t go all at once; it goes a row at a time. In the front row Caleb has had his pen going on the flyleaf of Hale’s book since Hale’s first sentence, and now the pen stops, and hangs over the page.
Jack looks at the clock. A minute forty.

Her hand hasn’t been near the left pocket. A dry cleaner’s tag is still pinned to that sleeve — Laney missed it — and from the third row he can see it turn over every time she lifts that hand, a small white flag, and he decides he will never tell her. In his chair Hale has closed *Brideshead* on one finger and stopped pretending to read it.

“The Professor tells you he’s never been paid,” she says. “Professor, where I come from we have a word for that.” She lets it hang just long enough. “It’s *grace*.” The hall goes up — Hale with it, his head back — and Jack sits on his hands.

“There’s a good man in the third row tonight,” she says. She says it straight down the aisle, at the third row, and looks the whole time at the exit sign over the back doors. Laney’s elbow goes into his ribs. His ears go hot. “Professor Hale says you don’t need a ghost to come collecting. He’s right about you. You never once waited for anybody to come collecting. You pay before the bill comes. You keep promises nobody’s checking on. I’m not asking you to believe a thing tonight. I’m asking you what you think you’re doing when you do that — because a man who pays every debt on time with nobody watching the books is either a fool, or he knows something about who keeps them. And you are not a fool.”
She doesn’t look at him while she says it, which is how he knows she means it.

body.text: “The Professor brought you a wolf,” she says. “I’ll take the wolf. A wolf that won’t hunt is a bad wolf. A broken one. But nobody in this hall would say that wolf *wronged* the pack, and you all know why.” She leans on Hale’s board, and it creaks. “A wolf can be damaged. Only a person can be wronged.” And over the quiet, lightly: “I got that from a dishwasher from Youngstown who plays Professor Hale better than Professor Hale.”

The hall laughs without knowing who she means. Hale, in his chair, inclines his head toward her, granting it. The hall has no idea, and two rows back Theo has every idea; he leans out past the sophomore and points at the back of Jack’s head at arm’s length, and holds the point.

“I found my creditor,” she says, “sitting across a table from me a week ago Monday. And I owe him the argument.” She leans on Hale’s board, and it creaks, and the hall laughs without knowing why, and Hale inclines his head to her.

“Somebody gave me my case a week ago Monday,” she says, “playing my opponent. He was supposed to be the Professor, and he couldn’t help himself.” She leans on Hale’s board, and it creaks, and Hale, in his chair, inclines his head to her.

“A week ago Monday Professor Hale asked me what I’d say to the good atheist in the third row. Here it is.” She leans on his board, and it creaks. “That he’s good, and that he’s owed, and that he owes — and I’d like to know to whom.”
“Professor Hale’s motion is a silence about who is owed.”

body: When she sits down it is nine minutes and some seconds by the clock, and the applause comes up out of the hall all at once and keeps on coming. She folds her hands on the table. The cards are still in the left pocket, where they have been all night. And only then, for the first time all night, she looks straight down the aisle at the third row.

s11b.slug: THURSDAY · 7:55 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — PICK A HORN
body: The rebuttals are four minutes each, and Hale takes his standing up and doesn’t walk. He stands at his own lectern with both hands on it and waits for the hall to finish settling. It does. It wants to know what he has been saving.

“There is a very confident young man in Plato called Euthyphro,” he says, “and Socrates spoils his whole afternoon with one question. I’d like to spoil Miss Broussard’s.” He doesn’t smile. “Is the good commanded by God because it is good? Or is it good because God commands it? If the first — the good stands above God, and God reads it off the same page as the rest of us, and my good man in the third row may go straight to the page and spare himself the bother of the middleman. If the second — the good is whatever God happens to want, and if he wanted cruelty, cruelty would be holy. Then you don’t owe a debt, Miss Broussard; you humor a mood. In very fine vestments.”

body.text: Jack threw it at her himself, a week ago Monday, in Hale’s voice, across the oak. It doesn’t sound like that in the man’s own.

body: He turns his head and looks at her down the length of the table.
“Pick a horn, Miss Broussard.”

The hall leans back toward him; Jack can feel it go. Up and down the rows people sit back. In the front row Caleb has a knuckle between his teeth. Beside Jack, Laney’s knee has started going up and down. There is a way out of it, and Jack knows where it is — Aquinas found the door seven hundred years ago, and Lena has read more Aquinas than Jack has read of anything — and none of that matters a damn when the house is watching your mouth.
And she stops.

It isn’t long. The second hand on the clock over the stage goes on one mark. But she stops, with her mouth open on the first word of something, and her eyes leave Hale and come out over the lip of the stage and down the aisle and find the third row.

choices.text: *Hold her eyes. Don’t look away.*
response: He holds them. He doesn’t nod or smile or do anything with his face that could be read from the stage as advice; he only looks back at her and lets her look, and keeps looking, with a hall full of people in the way and not one of them in the way. Whatever she came down the aisle for, she finds it, or decides she doesn’t need it. She looks back at Hale.

choices.text: *Look at your hands. Let her find it herself.*
response: He looks down at his hands on his knees — the cracks across the knuckles from three shifts a week in the Anchor’s sink, the burn on his thumb from the steam tray — and doesn’t look up, and the silence in the hall goes on past where he can stand it and keeps going. Beside him Laney’s knee has stopped bouncing. And from the stage, her voice, starting.

choices.text: *A Hail Mary, half aloud, for her and not the outcome.*
response: He says it the way he says it when he can’t think — fast, under the noise of the hall, the words worn smooth with use — and not for the vote, not for the cards in their boxes, not for Hale; for her, standing on a board that creaks with her mouth open in front of everybody. Laney hears him and doesn’t say a thing. “…now and at the hour,” he says, and on the stage she lifts her chin.

s11c.slug: THURSDAY · 8:05 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — THE THIRD HORN
body: “The Professor has offered me two horns,” Lena says. “I’ll take the bull.”
The laugh is half relief. She waits it out and comes forward off Hale’s board to the edge of the stage, so the stage lights catch the pearls.

“Neither. The good isn’t a rulebook nailed up over God’s head that he has to check, and it isn’t whatever he happens to feel like on a Tuesday. It’s what he *is*. Saint Thomas says God doesn’t *have* goodness the way I have this blazer — which is borrowed, and has to go back on its hanger by midnight. He is it. So when he commands, the command comes out of a nature. The way a promise comes out of a person. You don’t check a promise against a rulebook. You check it against who made it.” She looks out at them. “It’s like this. You don’t ask whether my mother’s love is good because she loves or loves because it’s good — you ask whether it’s *her*.”
In the third row Laney says *oh* under the noise, not to anybody.

Hale sits at the table with his pen stopped over his notes and looks at her across the stage, and the pleasure comes up into his long face whether he wants it there or not, and he opens his right hand on the table toward her, palm up, and leaves it open. He says nothing. Jack has never seen him give a point away without a word to soften the giving, and he doesn’t soften this one. He just leaves the hand there.
“Questions from the floor,” the Dean says. “One each. A question, please, not a speech. There is a microphone.”

There is: a stand in the center aisle at the foot of the stage. Hale gets up and goes to his lectern; Lena stays where she is, at the lip of the stage. Caleb is out of the front row and at it before she has finished, with Hale’s book left on his seat and an index card held in both hands, his clip-on tie gone slightly sideways. He bends to the microphone, which is set for somebody shorter, and it shrieks, and he jumps back from it, and the hall laughs, and he laughs too, too loud, and stops.

“Hi. Uh. Caleb Hargrove, I’m a freshman, philosophy. Hi, Professor.” Hale lifts two fingers off his lectern at him. “This is for Miss Broussard.” He reads it off the card, fast, in the Central Valley singsong that comes out of him when he’s scared. “If God is the creditor, why doesn’t he ever collect? Like — if the debt is real, if it’s actually owed to somebody, why does the somebody never show up for it?”
It’s a good question. Half the people in the hall came to hear somebody ask it. He’s finished, and he doesn’t sit down.

“Because,” he says, not reading now, “because, like — there was this guy. At our church. Back home.” The card goes down to his side. “He was the treasurer. And there was a building fund. Four years of a building fund. My mom did — there were so many bake sales, dude —” Somewhere up the back a laugh starts and doesn’t find anybody to go with it, and dies. Caleb doesn’t hear it. “And then one Sunday there’s, like, eleven people. In a room for three hundred. And my dad gets up there anyway, up front, same as always. And he looks out at all the — at all of it.” He stops. “And he smiled.”
He looks at the card in his hand. It’s in his own writing, and it doesn’t help him. He doesn’t finish.
Lena doesn’t move from the edge of the stage. When she answers him it’s quieter than anything she has said all night, and the hall has to go still to hear it, and does.
“I don’t know what happened to that man. I know the debt didn’t go away when nobody came to collect it. You know it didn’t.” She waits until he looks up at her. “That’s why you asked.”

Caleb stands there with the card. Then he nods at the floor, and goes back to his seat, and picks up Hale’s book off it and sits down with the book in his lap, and Yusuf, without a word, holds out the paper bag of seeds, and Caleb takes one and holds it.

s11d.slug: THURSDAY · 8:40 PM · SANDOVAL HALL 1 — THE SWING
body: The TAs come down the rows with shoeboxes. Jack puts in his red card. Laney kisses hers before she lets go of it, and leaves a print of the fire-engine lipstick on it, and says that’s so they know it was her. Down at the edge of the stage Evan Marsh and two other TAs kneel on the boards with the boxes upended between their knees and sort the cards into three piles, white and red and gray, while the hall talks too loud about nothing and stays leaning forward.
The Dean takes a slip of paper from Evan and comes to the side lectern. She doesn’t make them wait.
“For the motion, one hundred and forty-nine. Against, two hundred and one. Undecided, twenty-two.”

The hall takes the length of a heartbeat to do the arithmetic, and then it goes up. Laney is on her feet beside him screaming with both fists over her head, and two rows back Theo’s coffee can is going like a maraca, and halfway up the house Kevin is on his feet alone in the middle of his row applauding with his hands held up high in front of him, the way he would at a graduation.

Jack doesn’t get up. At her end of the table Lena has put both hands over her mouth, and over them her eyes go along the rows, counting, and he stays where he is in the third row and watches her do it. In the front row Caleb isn’t clapping. He sits with Hale’s book on the seat beside him and his cards in his lap, face down, and his hands flat on top of them.
Hale stands up at his lectern and waits, and the hall gives him his quiet, because he has earned it.
“The motion is defeated,” he says. “Deservedly.”

Then he comes out from behind the lectern and crosses the stage to her, past the water pitcher, and holds out his hand, and she gets up and takes it. He bends his head and says something to her, short, that doesn’t reach the third row. She says something back. He says one more thing and lets go of her hand, and walks off toward the wing with his hands behind his back. Whatever it was, Jack can see it land on her: she stands there after he has turned away with her hand still a little out in the air where his was.

At the back by the doors, Father Osei claps three times, slow, and turns to go. On his way out he looks across the emptying hall to the stage, and Hale, at the stage-left wing now with his jacket over his arm, looks back at him, and the two of them nod to each other across the empty seats, a short nod each way, wary and courteous. Osei goes out.

The Newman crowd comes down to the stage steps in a body — the band kids, Clare with her violin case on her back, the choir, a girl from Thursday Bible study in tears — and Lena is swallowed. Over somebody’s shoulder she finds him in the third row, and looks at him, and he looks back; then a soprano has her by both arms and pulls her round.

The hall is emptying up both aisles around him. Hale doesn’t stop for anybody: he goes out through the side door at the wing to the loading dock, and it swings to behind him. Up the center aisle Caleb is going the other way, fast, against the crowd, with his head down and his fist closed on something, out through the front doors into the dark.

choices.text: *Go out the side to the loading dock — Hale went that way.*
choices.key: After the Forum you followed Hale out to the loading dock.

choices.text: *Go out the front. Caleb went that way, fast.*
choices.key: After the Forum you went after Caleb.

s12c.slug: THURSDAY · 9:05 PM · SANDOVAL HALL, THE FRONT STEPS — BOTH CARDS
body: The front of Sandoval is all glass, and the lobby behind it is still lit and still full: people in coats who don’t want to go home yet, arguing in fours under the fire marshal’s sign, a philosophy TA with a box of leftover colored cards on his hip. The steps go down wide and shallow to the quad. Out at the bottom the Newman kids have made a knot under the lamp and are singing something with hand motions, and a sophomore with the *Tide* lanyard is trying to get a quote out of anybody at all.

Caleb isn’t in any of it. He’s at the far end of the steps, down against the planter where the light gives out, with Hale’s book beside him face down on the concrete. The clip-on tie is in his fist. In his other hand he has two of his three cards, one white and one red, held together like a hand at euchre he doesn’t want to play. The gray one is a crumpled ball on the step beside the book.
Jack goes and sits a step above him. Not close. He puts one hand flat on the concrete beside him and leaves it there.

“And it came to pass,” Caleb says to the quad, fast, the Visalia right up front in it, “that the multitude was divided, and lo, the against did rise by a hundred and three, and the professor said *Deservedly*, and it was so.” He holds the cards up without turning round. “I didn’t vote. Either time. I had this one in this hand and that one in that hand and I sat there through the entire count like a — dude, like a guy holding two cards. Front row. He could see me.”
“I saw.”
“Yeah. Everybody saw.” He opens his fist and looks at the tie in it, the little metal clip bent where he’s been working it. “She didn’t make him the bad guy.”
Jack waits.

“The treasurer. Every time I ever told that, he’s the bad guy. That’s the point of him. That’s his only job in the story.” Caleb bends the clip back the other way. “And she just goes, *I don’t know what happened to that man.* Like he was a man. Like he had a mom.” He laughs through his nose, with nothing in it. “My dad would have prayed for him. That’s worse.”

body.text: “Like I told you on the stairs. He never answered either. He just smiled.” It sounds exactly the same as it did on the stairs over the cove, and Jack doesn’t try to fix it any better now than he did then. He keeps his hand on the step.
body.else: He’s quiet a moment. Out on the quad the Newman kids get to a part of the song where everybody points at the sky. “I used to ask him,” Caleb says. “Why God didn’t do anything about it. Fifteen years old, every night at dinner, like it was my job.” He turns the red card over and back. “My dad never answered either. He just smiled.” Jack has never heard that before, and from the way it comes out he can tell it has mostly been said to ceilings. He doesn’t try to fix it. He keeps his hand on the step.

body: Caleb looks down at the two cards a long time. He pulls the red one off the white one, carefully, like they’ve been glued, and holds it back over his shoulder at Jack without looking.
“Give it to her,” he says. “Don’t say it’s from me.”
Jack takes it. It’s a plain red card the size of an index card, AGAINST printed across the top, a little soft at one corner from his thumb.

Caleb gets up all at once, shoves the white card in the book, the book under his arm, and goes down the steps two at a time and off across the quad, fast, the tie still in his fist, past the Newman kids without looking at them, out of the lamplight.

s12h.slug: THURSDAY · 9:05 PM · SANDOVAL HALL, THE LOADING DOCK — YOU ARMED HER
body: The side door at the end of the backstage corridor has a bar across it that says ALARM WILL SOUND, and the alarm doesn’t. It lets out onto a loading dock under one sodium lamp that makes everything look sunburned: the concrete lip, the black rubber bumpers bolted along it, two dumpsters, a stack of banquet chairs under a tarp. Past the dumpsters the Commons is shut for the night, a long low building with its EXIT signs burning green inside. The noise of a full hall leaving comes round from the front of the hall, cut down by the brick into something like surf.

Hale is sitting on the edge of the dock with his legs over and his jacket folded beside him, tie pulled loose, cuffs turned back twice. He has a flask in his hand, a flat silver one with a dent in its shoulder. He takes one pull off it when the door bangs, and screws the cap back on, and doesn’t offer it, and doesn’t look round.

body.text: “Mr. Costigan.” He doesn’t turn. “You armed her. A wolf. I gave you Foot for a week and you handed her a *wolf*.”
“Mr. Costigan.” He doesn’t turn. “You armed her. A creditor across the table — I recognized the furniture.”
“Mr. Costigan.” He doesn’t turn. “You armed her. You sat in my chair and gave her her case.”
“I armed her myself, Mr. Costigan.” He doesn’t turn. “A week ago Monday. With my own question. Remind me never to be generous again.”

body: Some vowel in it has gone short and northern, the way it does with him at the far end of a long day. Jack comes and stands at the edge of the light with his hands in the Carhartt and says nothing.

“I wrote you into my opening,” Hale says. “Did you notice? *The good man in the third row.* A rhetorical convenience. A figure. Somebody to be decent without a ghost to collect from him. And she turned round and addressed the figure by his seat number, and the whole hall looked at the back of your neck, and I lost the hall to a pair of ears.” He turns the flask over in his hand. “Sit where she can see you. I said that. I’d like it noted that I said that.”
“You did.”

“The horn business. Euthyphro. I have used that on bishops. I once used it on a Jesuit in Leeds and he had to go and lie down.” A car goes by on the service road with its radio up, and the bass of it thumps along the brick and away. “She went straight through the middle. I watched her look for you first.”
Jack looks at the dumpsters too.
Hale is quiet. Out of nowhere, with no performance on it anywhere: “She was always going to win it.” He looks at the flask and doesn’t drink from it. “I wanted to be the one she beat.”

Out front somebody is leading the Newman kids in a song Jack half knows, and the song falls apart into laughing. Hale gets up off the edge of the dock in two stages, a hand on the concrete, his knees reporting it, and shakes his jacket out and hangs it over his arm.
He puts the flask away in the jacket. “She’ll know anyway.”
“Yes, sir.”
Hale looks at him for that, the *sir*, with an eyebrow, and lets him have it. He goes to the side door and puts a hand on the bar and stops there.
“Monday, Waugh,” he says. “You may tell the table they are permitted to say *Thursday* again. I shan’t.” And he goes back into the building he lost in, holding the door behind him so it won’t bang.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 11:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — UNFORGIVABLE
body: By twenty past eleven Delgado has stopped being a building where something happened tonight and gone back to being a dorm on a Thursday. The tube light hums over her landing. Somewhere down on two a door opens on a television and shuts on it again.

She’s on her step with her flats on the step below her, side by side, toes out, shoes at a back door. The black blazer is off and laid across her knees like a lap rug. Laney’s pearls are gone — into a pocket, or back to Laney — but the medal is still outside her blouse where it was at twenty to six, lying on the white. Her lipstick is long gone too. Her hair has come half out of whatever it was in. She looks like she has been carried out of a hall on people’s shoulders and set down somewhere quiet and has not yet decided whether to sleep or to run around the block.
“There you are, Youngstown.”
“They let you go.”

“Peter Haddad made a toast with a Martinelli’s. In the lobby. Somebody had a *bottle opener*.” She moves the blazer over so there’s room on her step, and he sits, and her stocking foot comes over and rests on the toe of his boot and settles there. “Do you want to know what he said? Hale? When he shook my hand?”
“Yes.”
She looks straight ahead at the wired glass on two, black, with the two of them in it.

“He said, ‘You were very kind to my third row.’ I said I meant to be. He said, ‘I know. It was unforgivable.’” She lets that go up the stairwell. “And then he let go of my hand and walked off the stage with his hands behind his back, like he’d won. I am going to be up till three working out which half of that he meant.”

body.text: Jack takes the red card out of the side pocket of the Carhartt and holds it out. He doesn’t say anything about it. She looks at it, a red card with AGAINST across the top and nothing written on it, soft at one corner, and then she looks at him, and he watches her work it out — the front row, the question, the cards face down — and get there. She takes it in both hands. She holds it a long time, longer than the card needs. Then she reaches into the bag beside her, gets out her missal, opens it somewhere toward the back, lays the card in flat between the pages, and closes it, and keeps her hand on the cover.
She turns her head and looks at him instead of the glass, close, narrow-eyed, a woman checking a page for a hidden footnote. “You went out the side.”
“I did.”
“He said something about me.”
“He said you’d know.”
“I do.” She looks back at the glass. Whatever she knows, she keeps, and the keeping makes her sit up straighter on the step and look very pleased with the wired glass.

body: She kisses him then. She turns on the step and takes his face in her two hands and kisses him, and it isn’t for luck this time and it isn’t quick. The blazer slides off her knees and slithers down two steps and is left there. Her mouth tastes of sparkling cider and of nothing she put on for anybody. His hand goes to the back of her neck under the fallen hair, where it’s warm, and the medal is cold where it presses into his shirt, and she makes a small sound against him.

He wants her; it is the weather of him, top to bottom, and it is good, and it has an order to it he can feel like the grain of a step under his hand. Her first: the voice that took a hall apart and put it back together facing the other way, the stocking feet on cold concrete, the pulse going hard under his fingers at the back of her neck. Everything else after, and in its turn. He wants it all, and he is glad, tonight, to wait for it.

It goes on. It goes on until the tube light’s hum is the only thing in the stairwell that isn’t them. She’s the one who ends it. She draws back, not far, and lets her forehead come to rest against his, her eyes shut, her thumbs still at his ears.
She sits back on her own step and picks up her shoes, one in each hand, and remembers she has an agenda.
“Well, counsel? You had the third row.”

choices.text: “You had them at the debt. I counted. A minute forty.”
choices.key: On her landing after the Forum, you told Lena she’d had the room at a minute forty.
response: “You *counted*.”
“The clock over the stage. You said your first sentence and I looked up. A minute forty and Caleb’s pen stopped.”
“A whole hall, and you sat in the third row and *timed* me.” She points one flat at him like it’s loaded. “That is so *Ohio* I could spit.”

choices.text: “You were kind to Caleb. That’s what I’ll remember.”
choices.key: On her landing after the Forum, you told Lena that what you’d remember was how kind she’d been to Caleb.
response: She doesn’t answer him. She sets the shoes down again, side by side, toes out, and leans over and puts her head on his shoulder, and leaves it there.

He feels her stop being the woman who won and become a girl from Dupre Street who has been on her feet since six this morning. Her hair is against his neck. Her hand takes a fold of the Carhartt’s sleeve and keeps it.
She has her eyes shut. Whatever she’s seeing in there, it isn’t the hall.

choices.text: “With attribution.”
choices.key: On her landing after the Forum, you reminded Lena she’d won it with attribution.
response: “With *attribution*.” She puts one finger in the middle of his chest and pokes him with it, twice, hard, on the word. “I said I would. I said it in a seminar room in front of God and Yusuf. A Broussard doesn’t say *with attribution* and then not attribute.”
“The hall doesn’t know who you meant.”
“The hall doesn’t need to.” The finger doesn’t move from over his heart, pressing, holding a place in him like a place in a book.

choices.text: *Don’t give her a verdict. Sit with her.*
choices.key: On her landing after the Forum, you gave Lena no verdict at all, and sat with her.
response: He doesn’t give her one. He goes down two steps and gets the blazer and brings it back up and lays it over her knees again, and sits.

They sit. The television on two comes and goes again. After a while she starts telling him the night from the top, without being asked — Laney and the pearls, Margot’s headline, the Dean’s glasses on their chain, the board by Hale’s lectern that creaked exactly where she meant it to — and he lets her, every bit of it, like he wasn’t there.
Her voice goes on in the stairwell, low and fast and New Orleans, getting to the horns.

s14.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE FOURTH FRIDAY
body: In the inside pocket of the Carhartt, since ten past four, there is a three-pack of women’s white socks, size small, and a Barq’s going warm, both rung up at the Rite Aid on Mission by a cashier with a pencil behind each ear and a nametag that said ASK ME ABOUT OUR PHOTO CENTER.

By seven the Stations have stopped being something he goes to and become something he does on Fridays, like the dish machine on Saturdays at the Anchor. Four Fridays in, his knees know where the tile is. He knows which kneeler in the back rocks, and which acolyte walks the candles too fast, and that Gus Ferreira in the loft gives the chord a half-second early so the forty can find the note.

body.text: Bread and water since breakfast, both of them, and at this hour of a Friday it has stopped being hunger and become a kind of clearness, like the storm windows came down. Lena’s face has it too, under the black lace.
body.else: He had his meatless lunch at the Commons, fish sticks gone soft in their paper boat. She has had bread and water since breakfast, and at this hour of a Friday it shows in her face only as a kind of clearness, like the storm windows came down.

body: She came in at five to seven and sat in his pew without looking at him, as she does now, and when Father Osei came down the aisle in the purple stole behind the cross and the two candles, she stood when he stood. Her booklet is open on her palm. He reads off his own this time, and she notices, and doesn’t say so.

They go down the south wall. Between the stations Gus gives the chord and the forty walk to the next carving singing the old verse, *Through her heart, his sorrow sharing, / all his bitter anguish bearing*, and Lena is a little ahead of the beat again, and he is a little behind it, and they meet at the end of every line.

At the eighth, on the north wall where the candle smoke has got into the wood, Father Osei reads the name off the carving: *Jesus meets the women of Jerusalem.* “We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you.” Forty people go down on one knee on the tile. “Because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world.”

In the carving the women are a tangle of hands and veils at the edge of the road, kept back by a soldier’s spear held crossways, and he has turned his head to them under the beam. Father Osei reads it short, as he reads everything on Fridays, his eyes on the page: that they came anyway, that nobody asked them to, that he stopped on the worst road in the world to speak to them, and what he said was not *thank you* but *weep for yourselves and for your children*. Then he lets the church kneel on that.
Jack kneels on it. Beside him Lena’s lace has swung forward over her face, and her lips move a half-beat ahead of the forty.

Afterward the steps of St. Brendan’s are cold and clear, the second clear night running, and there’s no moon, and over the olive tree the stars go clear down to the hills. People come out past them buttoning coats. Lena folds the lace into a square and puts it in her pocket and comes down two steps and turns round to face him, so that she’s a little below him for once and has to look up.
“Tomorrow,” he says.
“Still?”
“Still.”
She narrows her eyes. “What do I wear?”
“Jeans. Something warm.”
“Jeans.” She says it like he has suggested a feed sack. “On a date.”
“It’s mine.”

She narrows her eyes further, and he can practically watch the sums go — jeans, warm, Saturday, the 11 runs till midnight, he said *mine* on Ocean Road and again on Monday — and come out to nothing, and her hating it, and loving it. She goes home still working it, her lips moving, and twice on Ocean Road she opens her mouth to ask him, and twice she shuts it.

s15.slug: SATURDAY · 5:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 217 — THE CARHARTT
body: The late sun comes down the second-floor corridor from the window at the end and lays itself along the linoleum to his boots. He knocks on 217 three times, evenly spaced. He did not practice it.
Laney opens the door with a hairbrush in her hand and her own hair half done, the other half still in rollers, and looks at him from his boots up, and turns round to the room.
“He’s in the *Carhartt*.”

He is. It’s Danny’s, the canvas faded to paper-sack brown, and he washed it Thursday night in the Delgado basement with a cup of somebody’s Tide, and it smells of that and of the dryer and, a long way under both, of five weeks without a cigarette. He has his good jeans on and his boots wiped, and that’s the outfit.

Lena comes to the door. Jeans, and a green sweater with the sleeves too long, and her jean jacket over it, and flats. Her hair is down, which it almost never is in the daytime, and it changes the shape of her, softer at the edges. She looks him over too, slower, and something happens at the corners of her eyes.
“You said warm,” she says.
“You’re warm.”
Laney points the hairbrush at him. “Where are you *taking* her?”
“Mine.”
“That is not a *place*.”
“It’s an address.”
Laney looks at the ceiling for help and gets none. She waves the two of them off down the corridor with the hairbrush, rollers bouncing. “Go. Be *poor* together.” The door of 217 shuts on her.

The 11 comes down Mission at dusk with its inside lights already on, so the town outside goes dim and blue and the bus is a lit box full of people going somewhere on a Saturday: two girls with a shopping bag between their feet, an old man with a folding cart, a kid asleep against the window with his headphones still going. Lena takes the window. He takes the aisle. Past the Anchor, past the Wharf Rat with its letters out, the sun is going down red into the haze over the water at the bottom of every cross street, one street at a time, like somebody turning pages.
He opens the RAZR to check the time and there’s Frank, from the afternoon, still sitting on the screen where he left it.

body.text: 2 OT. TURNER 31. FINAL TOMORROW.

body: Lena reads it over his arm without being invited, her chin on his shoulder.
“Evan Turner,” she says. “Thirty-one. I read the paper, Costigan.”

He turns his head to look at her. She has already gone back to the window, chin up, watching Mission Street go by toward wherever he’s taking her, pleased with herself the length of Mission, a woman who has waited all week for somebody to underestimate her.

s15a.slug: SATURDAY · 6:30 PM · MISSION LANES — LANE SIXTEEN
body: Lower Mission, past the tire place and the laundromat and the Mexican bakery with its pink boxes stacked in the window, there’s a neon bowling pin on a pole over a flat-roofed building the color of a Band-Aid. The pin’s head has been burned out for years, so from the bus stop it’s a white neon bottle with nothing on top. Under it, in letters that have survived better: MISSION LANES · SINCE 1961 · OPEN BOWLING · COCKTAILS · GRILL.
Lena stops on the sidewalk and looks up at it with her hands in the pockets of the jean jacket.
“Jack Costigan,” she says.
“It’s mine.”

Inside it’s loud in the way he wanted it to be loud: sixteen lanes in a row under a ceiling with boomerangs in the tile, and the long rolling thunder of balls going down the wood, and the crash at the far end, again and again, from every direction at once, so that under the noise nobody can hear anybody but the person beside them. The approaches are blond and gleaming. Over each lane hangs a screen, and at each scoring table an overhead projector throws the score sheet up onto it, somebody’s handwriting ten feet high in grease pencil. Along the back wall the league banners go back decades, felt letters on satin, MISSION MERCHANTS 1974, KNIGHTS OF COLUMBUS COUNCIL 2217, SATURDAY NITE MIXED. The air is lane oil and fryer and the popcorn machine by the door.

Ed Tavares is behind the counter under a television with a ball game on and the sound off: seventy if he’s a day, a cardigan buttoned wrong, hands like a pair of catcher’s mitts. He looks at Jack, and at Lena, and back at Jack.
“Sixteen,” Ed says. “Told you. The return sticks — kick it.”

He doesn’t ask their sizes. He looks down over the counter at their feet, one and then the other, and turns round to the cubbies and comes back with two pairs of rented shoes, red and blue and tan with the size on the heel in white paint, and sets them on the counter. Lena’s are a seven. Lena’s are right.
She picks hers up by the heels and looks at them, and then down at her flats, and at her bare ankles where the jeans stop.
Jack puts his hand inside the Carhartt, to the pocket on the inside over his heart, and takes out a three-pack of white socks, women’s small, still in their cardboard band. He holds them out.
“Ma’s rule,” he says. “You never put a bare foot in a rented shoe.”

She takes the package. She stands at the counter of Mission Lanes with a pair of red-and-blue bowling shoes in one hand and three pairs of white socks in the other, and looks at the socks, and her mouth opens a little and doesn’t produce anything. He watches something go up and down in her throat. On the television behind Ed somebody hits a shot from the corner and a crowd stands up without a sound.
“You bought me *socks*,” Lena says.

It isn’t a complaint. It isn’t a joke either, though she tries for a second to make it one, and can’t, and gives up. She looks at him over the package with her eyes very bright, and then she turns away to the molded orange bench by lane sixteen, and sits, and works the cardboard band off the socks with fierce attention, her head down, so he can’t see her face.

Lane sixteen is down at the end by the wall, as promised, with fifteen empty. The ball return stands at the head of it like a gumball machine with a grudge. He drops into the swivel chair at the scoring table, finds the grease pencil on its string, and writes on the clean sheet under the projector’s glass, in block letters, BROUSSARD, and under it COSTIGAN. Up on the screen over the lane, ten feet wide and wobbling a little in the heat of the lamp, her name goes up in his handwriting over his.
She looks up from her shoelaces and sees it, and stops.

“My dad bowled a league for twenty years,” he says. “Local 1112, Tuesday nights at the Valley Lanes out on 422. He averaged one-eighty-something, and I learned to keep score on his sheet with a grease pencil when I was nine.” He caps the pencil. “His ball’s in its bag in the basement, next to the Stroh’s fridge.”

He says it like the weather report from home. Lena doesn’t say she’s sorry. She looks up at her name on the screen. She ties her second shoe in a double knot, hard, and stands up in a pair of rented shoes and white socks.
“What do I do,” she says, “to beat you.”

She has bowled twice before: two birthday parties in Metairie when she was eight and nine, both with the bumpers up, and she remembers neither as a happy occasion. She tells him this while she walks the rack, lifting balls and putting them back. She chooses a fourteen-pound ball, marbled green, the heaviest one she can get off the rack with one hand, on the grounds that if she is going to be bad she means to be bad with conviction. She puts her fingers in the holes as if she’s taking an oath. She walks up to the foul line at a dead run and stops at it, and lets go from somewhere near her ear.

The ball goes into the left gutter about four feet out and travels the full sixty feet of it, slowly, with a sound like a long sentence that won’t be interrupted, and drops off the end without touching anything. Lena watches it the entire way with her hands on her hips.
“That lane,” she says, “is *crooked*.”

The return thinks about it, and keeps the ball. Jack gets up and kicks it at the base, where Ed said, and the green ball comes up out of the hole and rolls up the rack and knocks against the others, and Lena points at him across the approach.
“Don’t you *look* at me like that. Don’t you dare. I am warming up.”
Her second ball takes the seven pin, alone, from somewhere far out on the left, and she turns round with both arms up and the face of a woman who has just carried Orleans Parish.

His turn. He takes a twelve off the rack without having to look, because his hand still knows what a twelve weighs, and when he turns round she is already in the swivel chair at the scoring table with the grease pencil off its string, writing her seven up on the screen in a figure a foot high and underlining it. While he’s on the approach she says, to nobody in particular, “I hear Ohio’s very flat. I hear there’s nothing to do there but this.” He leaves the ten pin standing. She writes his nine up as a six. When he points at the screen she looks at it with the innocence of a cat and says the projector must be crooked too. She is sitting in his chair in white socks she didn’t own an hour ago, with his pencil, cooking his books in plain view of Ed Tavares, and he stands at the head of lane sixteen with his empty hand and lets her have all of it.

choices.text: *Teach her Frank’s way: walk it to the line, let go when your hand’s done.*
choices.key: At Mission Lanes you taught Lena to bowl the way your father taught you.
response: “Come here,” he says. “My dad’s way.”

He takes a ball off the rack and shows her with his own arm, not hers: four steps, not a run; the ball goes back by itself if you let it, like a pendulum, not like a throw; you walk it to the line and you let go when your hand is done and not before, and you don’t look at the pins. “Look at the arrows. The pins are going to be there. The pins can’t leave.”
“That’s just philosophy, Costigan.”
“That’s Tuesday nights on 422.”

She does it. Four steps, the green ball swinging back on its own, her eyes down on the little arrows, and she lets go low, and the ball goes out straight and true down the middle of sixteen with no hurry in it at all, and takes seven pins and leaves three standing like the last people at a wake. She turns round with both fists up over her head, rented shoes planted, hair everywhere, roaring, and doesn’t lower them, not for anybody, not even when lane fourteen starts to laugh.

choices.text: *Bowl for real. Tell her she’s terrible.*
choices.key: At Mission Lanes you bowled for real and told Lena she was terrible.
response: He bowls for real. His first ball hooks in late off the right and the pins go down in a pile like a dropped tray. He writes the X on the sheet, and it goes up on the screen, and he turns round.
“You’re *terrible*,” he tells her.
“I am *learning*, Costigan.”

She learns at the top of her lungs and with no technique whatsoever, and it costs him. By the second game she has worked out that she can’t beat him bowling, so she beats him talking: by the tenth frame she is narrating his approach as he makes it, low and urgent in the voice of a man calling a horse race at the Fair Grounds — *and Costigan comes up the stretch, the Ohio boy, the money’s all on him* — and he gutters twice in a row laughing so hard he can’t let go of the ball properly, and she puts a spare on top of it from God knows where, and when Ed’s projector adds it all up she has beaten him by one pin.
One. She stands under the screen and points up at it with both hands, and starts saying so, and he understands that she is going to be saying so until Easter at the very least.

choices.text: *Call it like Frank’s league — the frame-by-frame, the nicknames.*
choices.key: At Mission Lanes you called Lena’s frames like a league announcer and christened her the Mid-City Menace.
response: He calls it like the old men called it on Tuesday nights on 422, from the table, frame by frame, in a voice like a radio left on in a garage. “Broussard to the line. Fourteen-pound ball, which is a choice. She favors the left gutter, folks, she has always favored the left gutter, she was raised to favor it.”

She bowls a four and turns round to glare at him, and he’s already up and gone to the counter. Ed listens to him for three seconds and hands him the PA microphone off its hook without a word, with the look of a man who has been waiting since 1961 for somebody to ask.
“Ladies and gentlemen of Mission Lanes,” says the PA, all sixteen lanes of it, over the thunder, “now bowling on sixteen, out of Dupre Street, New Orleans, Louisiana — the *Mid-City Menace*.”

Lane twelve, a birthday party of women in their sixties in matching purple shirts, puts down their beers and applauds. Lena stands at the head of lane sixteen in rented shoes and white socks, blushing to the ears, and takes the bow: one hand on her stomach, one arm out, down to the knees, a Carnival-court curtsy.

choices.text: *Keep score. Let her find it.*
choices.key: At Mission Lanes you kept score and let Lena find her own way down the lane.
response: He doesn’t tell her anything. He keeps score. He writes her gutters as dashes and her one pin as a one, and sits in the swivel chair with the grease pencil and watches her work it out on her own. It’s the only way she has ever wanted to work anything out.

She tries running. She tries a little hop. She tries both hands and turns round and dares him to write it down. He writes it down. By the fourth frame she has slowed to a walk without noticing. By the fifth she’s stopped watching the pins and started watching the arrows, because she noticed lane fourteen doing it.

In the sixth she walks up, lets go low and late and easy, and the ball goes down the middle and takes eight. She doesn’t throw her arms up. She turns round, fast, to see whether he saw — her face wide open, checking, nothing held back from him.

s15b.slug: SATURDAY · 7:45 PM · MISSION LANES — THE SNACK BAR
body: The snack bar at Mission Lanes is a window cut in the wall at the end of Ed’s counter, with a flat-top grill behind it and a menu over it in white plastic letters pushed into black felt, a few of them crooked: CHILI DOG · NACHOS · GRILLED CHEESE · BURGER BASKET · ONION RINGS. There is no shrimp on it anywhere. Behind the window a small, wide woman in a Mission Lanes bowling shirt with CONNIE in red script on it works two spatulas at once, her reading glasses pushed up into her white perm, and when Jack comes up to the counter with Lena a step behind him she looks at him over the glasses and points a spatula.
“You’re the boy who came Monday and asked me about shrimp.”
Lena turns her head. “*Monday*?”

He orders two, dressed. Connie has them up in ten minutes, in red plastic baskets lined with wax paper, and while she sets them on the counter she tells Lena, one woman to another, as if Jack has gone to stand somewhere else: “He drew me a *diagram*. Lettuce, tomato, pickle, mayonnaise. He wrote *dressed* at the bottom and drew an arrow to it. I said, honey, I’m from Fresno.”
Lena carries her basket back to lane sixteen without a word. For Lena, that is a long way.

It’s shrimp on a hoagie roll from the Safeway, a roll that is doing its best: the shrimp fried hard in something out of a red can and heaped so high they fall off the sides, with shredded lettuce and two slices of a March tomato and pickle chips and more mayonnaise than the law allows. She sits in the swivel chair at the scoring table with the basket on her knees and turns the thing in her hands and examines it from three sides, a girl from Dupre Street in white socks and rented shoes, before she commits.
“It’s not a po’boy,” she says.
“No.”
“It’s a crime against my people.”

She eats every bite. She eats it leaning forward over the basket, so the shrimp that escape land in the wax paper and not on the jean jacket, and when hers is gone she reaches across without looking and takes the back half of his, and he slides the basket over to save her the reach.

He has carried the Barq’s since the Rite Aid on Friday. He takes it out of the Carhartt now and stands it on the scoring table at her elbow, by the projector, unopened. It has gone warm from riding against him all evening.

body.text: Lena stops chewing. She sits with the last of his hoagie in one hand and looks at the root beer standing there shut and warm by the hot white glass of the projector, and puts the hoagie down in the basket, and wipes her fingers on a paper napkin, slowly, one at a time. “For my hands,” she says. She sets her right hand on the table beside the Barq’s, not on it. For the rest of the night, whenever that hand isn’t busy with a fry or a ball or his sleeve, it goes back to the scoring table and rests there beside it, and she never opens it.
body.else: Lena picks it up and turns it to read the label. “*Barq’s*.” — “It’s from Biloxi,” he says. “Close enough.” She laughs at him — at Biloxi, at *close enough*, at a boy from Ohio who thinks Mississippi is next door to anything — and it still counts; he watches it count. She stands the root beer back by the projector, and when Connie calls across to ask does she want a cup of ice for that, she says no, ma’am, she’s keeping it.

body.text: Two games are up on the sheet under the projector glass, his 158 and 171, and under BROUSSARD a 71 and then a 94, which she has circled in grease pencil so it hangs ten feet high over the lane with a ring around it.
Two games are up on the sheet, and on the second her total is one pin higher than his, and she has drawn an arrow on the glass to it, so that the screen over sixteen points it out to the building.
Two games are up on the sheet, a 63 and an 80 for the Mid-City Menace, and Ed has read out both totals over the PA, and lane twelve has cheered both.
Two games are up on the sheet, and the second is an 88 she found frame by frame without a word from him, and every few minutes she glances up at it on the screen to make sure it’s still there.
Two games are done, and he has slid the sheet out from under the glass and folded it away, totals and all, which she calls a cover-up.

body: Sixteen is theirs till close; Ed waved one big hand at them when the second game ended and said it’s no good to anybody else. So they stay, with the baskets and the fries and the green ball on the return, and argue. They argue whether bowling is a sport. He says it is: it has a league, a ball, an average and a man who keeps it. She says it has vestments, a liturgy, an altar sixty feet long and a confessor named Ed, and she knows a sacrament when she’s wearing its shoes. They argue whether a strike is grace or work, and he says grace — you do everything the same and the seven pin stands there ten frames running, and then one night it goes down for no reason you did — and she says that is Calvinism and she will not have Calvinism said at her in a bowling alley; it’s habit, it’s Aristotle, Book Two, it’s walking it to the line a thousand times till your arm knows it the way your mouth knows the Our Father. They argue what Hale meant by *unforgivable* (her fourth theory since Thursday; this one involves Larkin and a hangover). They argue whether Connie could hold a grill for a week on Carrollton Avenue. Connie, yes. The bread, never. She steals his fries and he steals her onion rings back. She tells him his approach looks like he’s carrying a hot casserole out to a car. He tells her hers looks like she’s leaving a bar fight. She says thank you.

The jukebox stands by the door between the popcorn machine and a gumball machine that wants a dime: an old Rowe with its chrome going brown at the edges and the selections typed on little strips of card behind the glass. Eagles. Journey. The Doobie Brothers. Garth Brooks, three times. He found it on Monday while Ed was hunting for a pencil — the one New Orleans record on a California jukebox, one strip up from the bottom, the type faded but there — and he has kept a quarter apart from the rest of his change ever since, so it wouldn’t go into a bus fare by mistake. He gets up now and goes over and drops it in, and pushes the letter and the number, and behind the glass the arm travels down the rack and finds it.

The piano comes in over the thunder of fifteen other lanes, rolling, the left hand walking under it, and then the voice. Lena has a fry halfway to her mouth. She puts it down. She turns round in the swivel chair and looks at the jukebox, and then at him coming back across the carpet with his hands in the Carhartt, and her mouth opens, and shuts, and opens again.
“How much *thought* —”
“It’s two-fifty a game.”
“That is *not* what I’m talking about and you know it.”
She turns back round to the lane and hums the left hand with her eyes shut. He sits down at the table and keeps quiet for the length of the song.

Some time after eight it comes to him that the RAZR in the Carhartt hasn’t gone off all night — that he hasn’t felt it buzz, or gone looking for it, since the 11. He only notices because of the quiet where it would be. He leaves it alone.
When the record ends she swivels round to face him with her rented shoes up on the rail of the table and the Barq’s at her elbow, and studies him narrowly.
“Why bowling?” she says.

choices.text: “It was my dad’s. The league folded last spring, after the layoffs. I wanted to show you something that was ours before it all went.”
