response: She doesn’t say anything clever. For once she doesn’t say anything. She reaches across the scoring table, past the baskets and the grease pencil on its string, and puts her fingertips on the back of his wrist where the cuff of the Carhartt stops, and keeps them there while lane fourteen picks up a spare and the popcorn machine pops on by the door.

He looks down at her fingers on his wrist, a smear of grease pencil on the side of the first one, and then up at her face. At the counter, over the socks, she turned away so he couldn’t see it. This time she doesn’t turn anywhere. She sits in his swivel chair and lets him look.

choices.text: “Because it’s the only Saturday night I know how to do that’s mine.”
choices.key: When Lena asked why bowling, you told her it was the only Saturday night you knew how to do that was yours.
response: Lena takes that in. Whatever she was going to say back, something with an edge on it, she sets down next to the Barq’s.
“Then it’s a good one,” she says. “Do it again sometime.”

She gets up out of his chair and goes to the head of the lane and kicks the return at the base, where Ed showed them, because it has kept her ball again, and the green fourteen-pound ball comes up out of the hole and rolls up against the others. She lifts it off the rack in both hands, a free frame on a dead lane, and settles her fingers in the holes, and walks it to the line.

choices.text: “Last week I borrowed everything. This week I wanted the shoes to be the only thing that wasn’t mine.”
choices.key: When Lena asked why bowling, you told her that last week you’d borrowed everything, and this week you wanted the shoes to be the only thing that wasn’t yours.
response: It goes in, and she gets there — last Saturday’s borrowed jacket and tie, the roses in their cellophane, and tonight a pair of red-and-blue shoes with a 7 painted on the heel — and she laughs so loud, her rented shoes kicking at the rail of the table, that Connie leans out of the snack-bar window to see who’s dying.

“The *shoes*,” Lena says, when she can talk. “The only thing you rented tonight was the *shoes*.” She puts one white-socked foot up on the rail and admires it. “And these aren’t rented. These are mine.”
Connie looks at the two of them over her glasses, and shakes her head at her grill, and flips a patty, pleased.

choices.text: *Shrug. Bowl the next frame.*
choices.key: When Lena asked why bowling, you just bowled the next frame, and let her work it out.
response: He shrugs. He gets up and takes his twelve off the return and bowls a frame that isn’t on the sheet: four steps, and let go when the hand is done, and the ten pin left standing in the corner, and the spare on top of it. He comes back down the approach.
She has watched every bit of it with her chin up and her eyes narrowed, and by the time he sits down she has it worked out.

“It’s because it’s *loud*,” she announces. “You picked the loudest room in the county so you wouldn’t have to talk. That’s all right, Costigan. I talk enough for two.” She pats his knee in consolation and starts in on a story about a cousin of hers and a bowling alley in Kenner and a bet involving a live crawfish. She is wrong, and very pleased with herself about it, and he doesn’t correct her. He wouldn’t take this away from her for money.

s15c.slug: SUNDAY · 1:55 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — THE LOST HOUR

body.text: The score sheet is in her jean jacket now, folded in four: BROUSSARD over COSTIGAN in his capitals, and on her line a 94 with a spare in the tenth, the first spare she will admit to. It rode the 11 home in the Carhartt, and at the foot of the stairwell she held out her hand for it, and he gave it up.

The score sheet is in her jean jacket now, folded in four: BROUSSARD over COSTIGAN in his capitals, and her second game one pin over his, which he will maintain to his grave she talked him into in the tenth. It rode the 11 home in the Carhartt, and at the foot of the stairwell she held out her hand for it, and he gave it up.

The score sheet is in her jean jacket now, folded in four: BROUSSARD over COSTIGAN in his capitals, and the Mid-City Menace’s 63 and 80, as announced to all sixteen lanes. It rode the 11 home in the Carhartt, and at the foot of the stairwell she held out her hand for it, and he gave it up.

The score sheet is in her jean jacket now, folded in four: BROUSSARD over COSTIGAN in his capitals, and on her line the 88 she found by herself. It rode the 11 home in the Carhartt, and at the foot of the stairwell she held out her hand for it, and he gave it up.

The score sheet is in her jean jacket now, folded in four: BROUSSARD over COSTIGAN in his capitals, and two games of hers he has sworn on his mother never to read aloud. It rode the 11 home in the Carhartt, and at the foot of the stairwell she held out her hand for it, and he gave it up.

body: They have been on her landing three hours, talking about nothing. She’s on her step with her back to the cinderblock and her flats off, side by side on the step below, and her feet in the white socks lie across his knees where he sits sideways under her. The socks have gone dark at the heels from Ed’s carpet. The tube light hums over them both.

A boy from three has come up past them since, at one in the morning, with an orange traffic cone under his arm, and stepped over Lena’s flats very carefully, and looked down at the white socks across Jack’s knees, and said, “Nice socks, man,” and gone on up. Lena has been saying *nice socks, man* at intervals ever since, whenever there’s a lull, and there haven’t been many.

He has told her about the Valley Lanes out on 422: the carpet with planets on it, the cigarette machine by the door, the old men on Frank’s team who called him Frankie’s boy and let him write the frames, and the smell of the ball bag, the same as the trunk of the Silverado. She has told him about the bumpers in Metairie, and a girl named Brandi who cried when she lost, and how Lena, at eight, did not cry, and did not forgive.

They’ve done Nonna’s lentils — a spoonful each on New Year’s Day, for the money, every year of his life — and Lena wants to know, given Lordstown, whether the Costigans are doing it wrong or whether lentils are a fraud, and he says it’s a mystery of faith, and she says she will take it up with Nonna personally. They’ve done Mémère’s French, which is not Paris French and would like that understood. They’ve done what Mémère would say about a girl from Mid-City who can’t bowl. Lena does Mémère for it: she sucks in her cheeks and narrows her eyes and folds her hands on her stomach, a tiny old woman in a housedress on a porch in Breaux Bridge, and says, full of pity, “*Pauvre petite bête*.” Then she translates it for him — *poor little beast* — and does it again, because he asks. Nothing about the last three hours has been careful. She hasn’t checked his face to see how anything landed, and he hasn’t checked hers.
Twice in three hours she has come back round to Monday.
“You went out there on a *Monday*.”
“On the 11. At four.”
“And drew that woman a picture of a po’boy.”
“A diagram.”
“A *diagram*.” She looks at him from her end of the step with her feet across his knees, and doesn’t say the next thing. It’s on her face anyway.
“Where did you even *find* it?” she says, out of a silence, about something they finished with an hour ago.
“The record? Under Garth Brooks.”
“That poor man.” She shakes her head at the injustice of it. “Under *Garth Brooks*. Out here by himself.”

The RAZR lies open on the step by his hip, because she wanted to know how late it was and then forgot to look. His phone says 1:59. He looks at it, and back at her, and when he looks again his phone says 3:00.
She leans over his shoulder to see. “Where’d it go?”
“Arizona.”
“Arizona doesn’t *do* it.”
“That’s where it went.”

She sits back against the wall with her feet still across his knees, and for a little while she’s quiet. She hasn’t been quiet once in three hours. She looks at him. Her hair is down, the way it was at her door at twenty to six, and the stairwell light is no kinder to anybody than it ever is, and she doesn’t arrange herself for him at all.
“Nobody has ever thought this hard about me for two dollars and fifty cents.”

choices.text: “It wasn’t hard.”
choices.key: When Lena said nobody had ever thought this hard about her for two-fifty, you told her it wasn’t hard.
response: “That’s what I mean,” Lena says.

She swings her feet down off his knees and leans down off her step and kisses him, and it’s hers, and slow, slower than anything she has done all night. Her hand comes to the front of the Carhartt, over the pocket where her score sheet rode home, and takes a fistful of the canvas, and keeps it.

When the kiss is done she doesn’t let go of the jacket. She sits back on her step holding on to a handful of Carhartt and looking at him, with her hair down and her socks dark at the heels, and gives no sign of ever meaning to give it back.

choices.text: “I’ve been thinking about the socks since Thursday.”
choices.key: When Lena said nobody had ever thought this hard about her, you admitted you’d been thinking about the socks since Thursday.
response: She laughs at the socks, and at Thursday, and at whatever she is picturing — him, a Rite Aid, an aisle of hosiery, a decision about sizes — and partway through she kisses him in the middle of it, so the kiss still has the end of the laugh in it and he can feel it go through her.
After, she puts her forehead down against his collarbone, on the canvas, her feet still across his knees, and her shoulders go on shaking a little into the Carhartt.

choices.text: “Five. There were two games.”
choices.key: When Lena said nobody had ever thought this hard about her for two-fifty, you corrected her — five dollars; there were two games.
response: “*Five*,” she says. “Lord have mercy.”
She leans down and kisses him once, hard, both hands on his face, a kiss with a period at the end of it. He has nothing further.

She swings her feet down and picks up her flats by the heels and goes down the half flight to two in the white socks, and at the bottom, with one hand on the wired-glass door, she turns round and holds up the other with all five fingers spread.
“Five,” she says.

choices.text: *Kiss her. Say nothing.*
choices.key: When Lena said nobody had ever thought this hard about her, you didn’t say anything — you kissed her.
response: He leans up to her from the step below and kisses her, and it’s his, and it isn’t an answer to anything; it’s just the only reply he has that’s the right size. She tastes of the Tic Tac she dug out of the bottom of her bag on the 11. Her hand goes into the hair at the back of his head. Somewhere over Arizona their hour is going on without them, and neither of them sends for it.
When it’s done she sits back against the cinderblock with her feet still across his knees and looks at him with her lips a little apart.
“Well,” Lena says. It seems to be her complete opinion on the subject, and he can’t improve on it.

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — ROSE
body: Every face at the 11:30 is an hour short. The clocks went forward at two, and the parish has come up Ocean Road in the sun with its eyes not quite open: a father in the back pew asleep sitting up with a sleeping baby on him, an usher yawning into the collection basket, and Lena beside Jack on the Mary side with her lace on, who got to bed at a quarter past three by the new clock and is not prepared to discuss it.

Father Osei comes up the aisle behind the cross in rose. After three Sundays of purple it lands on the eye like warmth, an old, soft color with gold at the hem, and it doesn’t say the fast is over. It says *halfway*, and *keep going*, and *look up*, for one Sunday. The flower stands that have been bare since Ash Wednesday have something in them again, pink and white stock out of somebody’s garden on the Mesa, and up in the loft Gus Ferreira, who has been playing Lent with one hand behind his back, pulls out every stop the season allows and lets the organ go. There is still no Gloria. The organ doesn’t mind; it had the procession.

The first reading is somebody new, a Newman freshman with a fresh haircut who holds the lector’s binder against his chest with both hands and says *Gilgal* three different ways and gets the rest exactly right. The Israelites keep the Passover on the plains of Jericho, and the next day they eat what the land grows, and that same day the manna stops. No more bread out of the sky. From then on they eat the yield of the land of Canaan. The boy reads it as though it’s good news, and Jack supposes it is: the miracle quits because it isn’t needed anymore, and now they have to farm.

Father Osei reads Luke. The tax collectors and sinners drawing near to listen, and the Pharisees grumbling that this man welcomes sinners and eats with them; and so the story. The younger son who wants his half now, and gets it, and goes off and spends it, and ends up feeding somebody else’s pigs and wanting what the pigs eat. *Coming to his senses.* The long walk home with a speech ready in his mouth. And the father, who sees him a long way off and runs — a man with land and servants, hitching up his robe and running down the road in front of the village, which a man like that did not do — and is on the boy’s neck before the speech is half out. The robe, the ring, the sandals, the calf. And out in the field the older son, coming in at dusk and hearing music from the house, and asking a servant what it is, and standing in the yard and refusing to go in. Somewhere in the middle of it Jack thinks of a letter in his desk drawer, addressed to Trumbull, and then he is listening again.
Father Osei comes down to the step with his hands folded and looks out at three hundred people an hour short.
“The father goes out twice: once to the son who ran away, and once to the son who stayed and is angry. The second walk is the longer one.”
He goes back to his chair. The church sits with it. At the back the baby wakes and says one loud word that isn’t one, and is hushed.

Two pews up, on the aisle, Kevin is by himself in his good jacket. When Jack turns at the Offertory to watch the gifts come down, Clare Dominguez is at the rail of the loft with the band kids and her violin, playing under Gus. At the sign of peace Kevin turns round in his pew to the old man behind him, a man in a Korea cap with a cane hooked over the pew in front, and holds out his hand; the old man takes it in both of his and says something Jack can’t hear, and Kevin nods.
Lena turns to Jack.
“Peace be with you.”
“And also with you.”

It’s the handshake, the same as last Sunday and the Sunday before — except that along the side of her first finger there’s still a smear of grease pencil from lane sixteen that a Saturday night’s soap didn’t get, and she holds on to his hand longer than last week. All around them the church is reaching across pews. He doesn’t remark on it. She doesn’t either. She lets go when the Lamb of God begins, and folds her hands, and the grease pencil is on the outside of them, where he can see it.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S COURTYARD — ST. JOSEPH
body: The coffee urns are steaming on their folding table under the olive tree, and the sprinkler is off again, two Sundays running, and the Knights of Columbus have brought donuts in pink boxes from the place on Mission. Over by the gate Father Osei, still vested, is shaking hands and being told about the clocks by every person who passes him, as though he might have had a hand in it. Lena has a powdered one and a styrofoam cup and her lace still on her hair. She has forgotten it’s there.

He tells her his grandmother’s question instead. Ma passed it on last Sunday, and he has been meaning to ask all week and kept not asking, because asking means making something of Friday: do they do the table out here.
“What table?”

body.text: “St. Joseph’s. Friday.” He looks into his coffee.
“St. Joseph’s. Friday’s St. Joseph.” He looks into his coffee. “It’s my birthday.”

body: Lena stops with the donut halfway to her mouth. Powdered sugar sifts down off it onto her black flats.

body.text: “I *know* what Friday is,” she says. “Mémère put it on the back of a holy card in February, Costigan, and I stood in the door and translated. Did you think I’d forget?”
“I didn’t want a fuss.”
“You were born on St. Joseph’s Day,” she says, “and you didn’t *tell* me?”
“I’m telling you.”

body: “Costigan. I am from New *Orleans*.” She sets the coffee down on the corner of the folding table to free a hand for this. “Every Italian church in that city builds an altar on the nineteenth of March you could see from a plane. Three tiers. Bread baked in the shape of his staff, and his beard, and his sandals. Fig cookies. Lemons. The lucky beans — you keep one in your wallet and you’re never broke a day. We used to go round to six, seven altars in an afternoon, and I’m not even Italian, and you were *born* on it, and you were going to let it go by with what? A cupcake? In the *lounge*?”
He opens his mouth.
She holds up the donut to stop him, and looks at him over it, and he watches her decide something, fast.
“Leave it with me.”

choices.text: “Don’t go to any trouble.”
response: “Costigan, it is a *feast*. Trouble is the point.”

She has the enV out of her jacket before he can argue, flipped open, the donut parked in her teeth and both thumbs going on the little keyboard, and from the set of her eyebrows he would bet his Saturday tips it’s Laney.

choices.text: “Is there cake?”
response: “There are fava beans.”
“That’s not cake.”

“It’s *better* than cake. It’s a bean that saved Sicily.” She says it with her chin up, triumphant, and a small white smudge of powdered sugar on the point of it that he decides, there under the olive tree, not to mention.

choices.text: “We haven’t done anything for it since Danny went away.”
response: She doesn’t answer that. She takes his hand, there under the olive tree in front of the Knights of Columbus and the pink boxes and the urns, and keeps it, the donut forgotten in her other hand and the sugar coming off it onto the flagstones.

He looks down at their two hands. Hers is smaller than he keeps expecting, and warm from the cup, and she doesn’t let go of his while one of the Knights comes by with the pink box and Jack takes a donut one-handed, or after, when the urns run dry.

body: He can see the living room on Glenwood without trying: the recliner, the set too loud, a can of Stroh’s on the arm, and Frank on his feet for the last two minutes of a twenty-nine-point game, because you don’t sit down for a championship, you never know.

body.else: She does the weather on Glenwood, and Father Dom’s cold, and the Vitales’ gutters. “And Saturday?” Ma says. “Where’d you take the girl?” — “Lena, Ma.” — “Lena,” she says, trying it out. “Where’d you take Lena?”

body: “Bowling, Ma.”
There is a silence on Glenwood Avenue long enough that he takes the RAZR away from his ear to see if he’s lost her.
“Your father took me bowling,” Ma says. “Our second date. I bowled a forty-one and he married me anyway.”

In nearly nineteen years he has never heard this. He sits on the step with the phone against his ear and tries to see it — Ma in a pair of rented shoes, Frank with all his hair, a grease pencil — and can’t, quite, and wants to.
“I brought socks,” he says.
“*Good* boy.”
He tells her Lena’s doing the table on Friday. He tells her Lena said to leave it with her. Behind Ma, close to the phone, Nonna says something with *fave* in it, and then, sharp: “*Lei lo sa?*”
“She wants to know does the girl know about the beans.”
“She knows more than me, Nonna.”

Ma tells her. In the kitchen on Glenwood there’s a pause, and then a chair scraping back to the table, which from Nonna is a blessing. “Your father watched the whole thing standing up,” Ma says. “Eat something.” And she’s gone.

s19.slug: SUNDAY · 9:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, HIS STEP — ¶31
body: Ten past nine on a Sunday is the quietest the stairwell gets all week, everybody behind a door with the reading they didn’t do on Saturday. Jack is on his step, third down from four, with the four-dollar Catechism open on his knee to paragraph thirty-one. *Ways of Coming to Know God.* The Post-it is inside the front cover where he stuck it on Thursday, *¶31. PROOFS. WED.* The stranger who owned the book before him wrote *yes* in the margin a page back, by thirty, and then stopped, so from here on the margins are his. He has a pencil stub from the cup on Ed Tavares’s counter. So far he has underlined one thing — that these ways get called proofs, but not the kind a lab means — and written nothing beside it. He has three days, and he would like to walk into Wednesday with something better than Aquinas’s greatest hits.

Lena comes up from two with her own book. It’s the Waugh, Hale’s fresh copy, *Brideshead* with the spine not broken yet, and she has a pencil of her own behind her ear. She sits down on the step below his, sideways at first, and then not: she leans back until her back is against his shins, and opens the book on her knees, and reads. He can feel her settle through the denim. She reads fast, like she does everything, and every few pages the pencil comes out from behind her ear to put a mark in Hale’s clean margin — a tick, a question mark, a word he can’t read upside down — and goes back. Down on two somebody’s television laughs at something.
The RAZR is on the step beside him. It lights.

body: He picks it up and reads it. Then he leans forward and turns the screen round and holds it down past her shoulder, where she can see it.
Lena reads it. She hands the phone back up to him.
“Then do the reading.”
She turns a page of Waugh and goes back in.

He folds the phone shut and sets it down on the step, and does the reading. He reads thirty-one again from the top, slowly, and then thirty-two: the world, starting from motion and becoming and contingency, its order and its beauty, and how a person might come by those roads to the God who is its beginning and its end. The pencil stub makes a mark in the margin, and then another.
Below him Lena reads on. When he turns the page, the paper loud in the quiet, she tips her head back against his knee, her eyes still on her book, and rests it there.
